title: CPAT-AI Documentation
text:
Foreword

Why CPAT-AI?
The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), developed jointly by the World Bank and the IMF, gives governments a rapid assessment of climate mitigation policies: their effects on energy prices and use, emissions, government revenue, GDP, air pollution and health, transport and households, for more than 180 countries. Its methodology is set out in the CPAT Documentation, the companion volume on this site.
CPAT is a large spreadsheet model. It has grown over many versions and many hands, and like any model of its size it contains formulas that do not compute what they were meant to, and modelling choices that are open to question. Both are hard to find in a workbook of tens of thousands of rows.
CPAT-AI is the project that rebuilds CPAT so that every number can be traced, checked and explained. It replicates the legacy model module by module, finds and documents its bugs with cell-level fix plans the CPAT team can apply to legacy CPAT, tracks every open modelling question, and extends the model where the team decides to. The work is done with AI coding agents under explicit written norms, and every step is checked by independent recomputation.


What is in CPAT-AI
The project has two models that share the same inputs, codes and data:

Excel-AI: Excel prototypes generated by Python builders. The mitigation prototype is the integrated model; the distribution module and the air-pollution module are standalone workbooks linked to it.
Coded CPAT: a component-based Python reimplementation of CPAT, with a Shiny application. Validated Excel prototypes are ported to it once checked.

Legacy CPAT is the reference for both. Every difference from it is either a fixed bug, a replicated and tracked issue, or a departure the team decided on.

title: 1  Project overview
text:
How the work proceeds

Replicate. A block of legacy CPAT is rebuilt in the prototype, formula by formula, with the same sections and the same codes.
Check. An independent Python recomputation of the block reproduces every number; the prototype’s result is compared with legacy’s stored results.
Classify every difference. A difference is either a legacy bug (fixed in the prototype, with a cell-level fix plan for legacy), a legacy issue (replicated and tracked), or a departure decided by the team (tracked).
Release. The builder writes a new version; the quick check, the paste test and the regression against the previous release must pass; the register documents, the tracker, the codes map and the deck are regenerated.
Port. Validated blocks of the Excel prototype are ported to Coded CPAT.

title: 2  Bugs and issues
text:
Definitions
The rule applies to every model of the project, in Excel and in Python. It keeps the prototypes faithful to legacy CPAT where legacy does what it means to, and correct where it does not, and it makes every difference from legacy visible.
Data problems are issues. They are replicated. Where legacy needs a formula fix to handle the data correctly, that fix is a legacy bug (L) with a cell plan and the issue is ranked Very high; where no cell plan is possible, the prototype aligns with legacy exactly and the issue is ranked Extremely high.

title: 3  The mitigation prototype
text:
1. What it is
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Documentation.md.
The short guide. Details of every block: the Methods volume. Every legacy bug and issue: the bug-fix register.
The mitigation module of the IMF/World Bank Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), rebuilt as one readable Excel workbook for one country at a time.
It answers: what do carbon pricing and related policies do to energy prices, energy use, emissions, government revenue and GDP, year by year to 2041?

title: 3  The mitigation prototype
text:
Policies in: carbon tax, a new emissions trading system (ETS) with a cap, feebates, fuel excises, fuel subsidy reform, a methane fee, existing carbon pricing, power-sector policies.
Results out: retail energy prices, fuel use in 16 sectors and 8 fuels, electricity generation and prices, revenue, CO₂ and other greenhouse gases, local air pollutants, GDP effects, the gap to the country’s NDC, and household effects by decile (Distribution tab).
One country, any country: formulas contain no country numbers. Every country value comes from the data tabs, looked up by the country code on Settings (C4). The shipped data are complete for Egypt.
Same as legacy, minus its bugs: it follows legacy CPAT except where legacy has a bug (all fixed) or an open question that we track (issues). See section 5.
Readable and checked: every formula is at most 100 characters and one formula serves a whole block of cells. An independent Python recomputation checks every number.

title: 3  The mitigation prototype
text:
2. Quick start

Open CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm (in excel_ai/; the same file as excel_ai/permalink/CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_latest.xlsm) in Excel 365 with macros enabled. It opens on ScenarioCompare, the dashboard, without recalculating: the file ships with its values, in manual calculation.
After any change, click Recalculate now (or switch automatic calculation on with Recalculation on/off).
Read the results on ScenarioCompare. Choose Live or Stored results and the year. The key table shows CO₂, GHGs, revenue, the GDP effect and welfare against the baseline; the charts show them over time.
Change a policy on ScenarioDefinition. Column K is the live scenario: for example change CPLevelTarget (carbon price in the target year), then Recalculate now.
Store several scenarios: copy a definition one column to the right, give it a short name (row 2) and Run? = Yes (row 4), then click Run stored scenarios. Results go to StoredOutputs; the dashboard compares up to 10.
Update the data from the data workbook: choose the source on ScenarioCompare, click Update data tables. The status is on Cover.
First time only: click First-run test (grey buttons). The check table must show PASS.

The tabs, left to right: the front (Cover, ScenarioCompare, ScenarioDefinition), the model (Mitigation, Distribution, LiveOutputs, StoredOutputs), the inputs (Manual inputs, Settings, Inputs), the data tabs (legacy tables, unchanged), and the reference tabs (version log, differences with legacy, variable dictionary).

title: 3  The mitigation prototype
text:
3. How it works
The Mitigation tab runs top to bottom, one section per step, with the section numbers of legacy CPAT. Each scenario is a group of columns: group 1 is the baseline, group 2 the live scenario. Years run across, 2022 to 2041.

3.1 Policies (section 1)
Each policy is a path from a start year to a target year, set per scenario on ScenarioDefinition. The carbon price follows that path:
τ(t) = path(t; start year, target year, start level, target level) · (CPI index if the inputs are nominal)
A new ETS starts at a price estimate and is checked against its cap (the goal seek refines it). Feebates act through a shadow price, which changes efficiency but raises no revenue. Existing carbon taxes and ETS prices come from the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard data.
Details: Methods, chapter Prices; chapter ETS.


3.2 Energy prices (section 2)
For each fuel and sector, the retail price builds up from the international price:
supply cost  C(t) = fixed part + (C(t−1) − fixed part) · international price(t) / international price(t−1)
retail price R    = (C + excise and other taxes) · (1 + VAT)
after policy P    = R + new carbon tax + ETS price + new excise, each with VAT
Subsidies are negative taxes. Historical prices come from the IMF price data up to the last historical year (2022, as legacy); later years are projected.
Details: Methods, chapter Prices.


3.3 Energy demand (sections 5-8, 11)
Fuel use in each sector changes each year with income, its own price and efficiency:
Q(t) = Q(t−1) · (efficiency gain) · (1 + GDP growth)^(income elasticity) · (P(t)/P(t−1))^(price elasticity) · (efficiency response to prices)
The elasticities are legacy CPAT’s. Section 11 adds up fuel use by sector and fuel, including the fuel burnt in power plants.
Details: Methods, appendix A (equations, section 4); chapter Transport for road.


3.4 Power (section 3)
Electricity demand comes from the sectors. The power model, as legacy’s engineer model, decides each year:

Dispatch: which plants run, by their variable cost (fuel, carbon price, operation).
Investment: new capacity by technology, chosen by levelised cost with a logit share, within scale-up limits.
Prices: electricity prices from the cost of generation, with taxes, subsidies and price controls.

Power-sector policies (no new coal, nuclear from a year, renewable subsidies, PPAs, rebating revenue, an electricity excise) are set per scenario.
Details: Methods, chapter Power.


3.5 Road transport (sections 5, 5b)
By default road fuel use follows the demand elasticities, as every other sector. With TrModel = Engineer, the road engineer model replaces it: vehicle stocks by class, cost of ownership, the choice between combustion and electric vehicles, and vehicle policies (feebates, EV subsidies, purchase taxes, distance tax).
Details: Methods, chapter Transport.


3.6 Revenues (section 12)
Revenue is fuel use times the tax per unit, by fuel and sector, for existing taxes, existing subsidies (negative) and new policies:
revenue from new policies = fuel use · (carbon tax + excise + auctioned share · ETS price + VAT on them)
total revenue             = existing taxes + subsidies + new policies + methane fee
The power sector adds its own revenue and subsidies. Feebates are revenue neutral.
Details: Methods, chapter Macro and results.


3.7 Emissions (sections 13-15)
CO₂ = fuel use · emission factor        (factors optionally calibrated to the GHG inventory)
Other greenhouse gases (methane, nitrous oxide, F-gases) follow their drivers; methane from fuel supply responds to the methane fee. Local air pollutants (fine particles, sulphur and nitrogen oxides, and others) are fuel use times pollutant factors.
Details: Methods, chapter Emissions.


3.8 GDP, carbon pricing indicators, welfare (sections 16-18)
New revenue is fiscal space. How it is used (tax cuts, investment, transfers) moves GDP through fiscal multipliers, one year later:
fiscal space fs(t)  = (new revenue in the scenario − in the baseline) / GDP
GDP effect          = Σ over uses: share of the use · Σ over lags (change in fs · multiplier of the use)
Section 17 reports carbon prices and coverage; section 18 the welfare effects and the gap to the NDC.
Details: Methods, chapter Macro and results.


3.9 Distribution (tab Distribution)
Household effects by decile in one analysis year: price changes reach households directly (energy) and indirectly (other goods, through the input-output table); revenue recycling (transfers, targeted by ASPIRE or the poverty line) offsets them.
Details: Methods, chapter Distribution.

4. Results and the dashboard
ScenarioCompare is the place to read results:

Choices: Live (the scenario groups of Mitigation) or Stored (every stored scenario), and the year.
Key table: energy CO₂, GHGs, revenue, GDP effect and welfare, as levels and differences from the baseline.

title: 3  The mitigation prototype
text:
5. Limits and differences from legacy
The rule: never replicate a legacy bug; always replicate a legacy issue, and track it. A bug (L) is legacy computing what it does not intend; the prototype fixes it. An issue (I) is legacy doing what it means to, where the choice is open to question; the prototype does the same. Problems of the input data are issues too (area Data): where legacy reads the data wrongly, the formula fix is a bug with a cell plan and the issue is Very high; where no cell plan is possible, the prototype does exactly what legacy does and the issue is Extremely high (Appendix B). Every item has a code; the codes are explained in Appendix A.

Legacy bugs: the prototype fixes every one, in every module (mitigation, distribution, the inputs). The bugs, with the cell-level fix for legacy CPAT and the status of each in the latest legacy file CPAT 1.0pre_465, are in excel_ai/Legacy_CPAT_Bugs_v<version>.docx; the master list of bugs and issues is the tracker excel_ai/Tracking_Legacy_Bugs_v<version>.xlsx.
Issues (data problems first), departures, prototype bugs and upgrades: the appendices below (and the tracker, tab Issues).
Legacy row numbers in the Methods volume are rows of CPAT 1.0pre_456_NoPropData.xlsb, the file the prototype was built and checked against (its data extracts read that file). In CPAT 1.0pre_465 Mitigation rows from 5667 on sit 11 to 15 rows higher. The input sheet ScenarioDefinition has the rows of the 465 MTInputs.
Not built: a few legacy features (upgrades, Appendix E), and the air-pollution co-benefits and transport externalities modules.
Data: the shipped data are Egypt’s; proprietary tables for other countries must be pasted in or linked (issue I90).

0. Assumptions: what the numbers mean
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Prices.md.
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
How the model projects fuel supply costs and retail prices, following legacy CPAT cut down to the basics, and the existing carbon pricing on top of them (section 5b). title: 4  Prices and energy demand
text:
#
Assumption




A1
Every price, tax and policy value is in real US dollars of the results year (ScenarioDefinition ResultsYear, 2026, from scenario 1), per GJ. A constant real price is a constant number. There is no inflation after the conversion, and fuel use responds only to real price changes.


A2
Two indices, both 1 in the results year. The CPI index (US CPI of the results year / of the year) converts nominal domestic values; the deflator index (US GDP deflator, same form) converts nominal international prices. This is the legacy split (CPI rows 456/725, deflator row 467; row 630 is its reciprocal). Up to 2030 they differ by up to 1.2% (2022: 1.137 vs 1.124; 2030: 0.918 vs 0.929), so one index would not reproduce legacy.


A3
Domestic price data are nominal USD of their own year (IMF price dataset, Prices_dom: supply cost, excise and other taxes, retail price). Each is converted with that year’s CPI index and divided by GJ per price unit. Units: $/liter for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene; $/bbl for other oil products; $/GJ for coal, gas and biomass.


A4
Forecasting coefficients are base-year (2022) nominal values: the margin over international prices and the domestic production cost. They are converted with the 2022 CPI index and held constant in real terms. (coded applies no conversion here; to check against legacy in bucket 5.)


A5
International prices are nominal by source (IMF, WB, IEA, EIA, averages, Manual: IMF to 2025, then sheet Manual inputs D221:AF225 at the legacy addresses, by label and year), converted with the deflator. Only their year-on-year ratio moves the supply cost, so their units and level drop out. Beyond a source’s horizon the data hold them constant in real terms.


A6
ScenarioDefinition policy inputs are real (results-year USD): the carbon price, feebate rates and fuel price reform increases (in price units, e.g. $/liter real). Only the carbon price has a nominal option: NomorReal = Nominal makes the path nominal, then multiplied by the CPI index (legacy row 2249).


A7
History vs projection. Prices up to the last historical price year (Settings C10; default 2022, as legacy) come from data; later years are projected. Fuel use is data in the base year (2022) and modelled from 2023. The IMF dataset also holds 2023-2024; setting C10 to 2024 uses them (issue I89).


A8
Global vs per scenario. Global (Settings, ScenarioDefinition scenario 1): results year, government price controls (pass-through), last historical year, the country’s gas market. Per scenario: international price source and High/Low adjustment, carbon price and its nominal/real switch, fuel price reform, feebates, coverage.


A9
Horizon. Values after 2030 are not compared with legacy. The legacy CPI is held flat after 2031 (WEO horizon), the deflator is not, and some legacy rules (A10) misbehave over long horizons. The model computes to 2041 (the legacy horizon of the power block), but 2031-2041 are not a target.


A10
Legacy rules are copied as they are, except the bugs. v0.4.10 (user rule: bugs are never replicated): legacy bug L14 is fixed: with pass-through 0.5 or 0.8, legacy’s other taxes jumped in the first projected year (the floating subsidy multiplied by (1 - pcc) a second time); the prototype applies (1 - pcc) once (no effect for Egypt, pass-through 0 or 1). Changed (user decision): other oil products are treated like the other oil products, taking pass-through and margin from the dataset (Egypt: 0 and 7.95 $/bbl) instead of the legacy hardcodes 1 and 0. Under the legacy rule their retail price fell with the oil price to the 0.01 floor (3.79 $/GJ in 2024, 0.23 in 2030), and their fuel use rose 10x by 2030.


A11
VAT rate (user decision). Use the dataset’s VAT rate where it is filled. Otherwise use the country’s general VAT rate (Egypt 14%) for residential coal and gas and the all-sector oil products (gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, other oil products), and 0 for power, industry (VAT is credited to firms) and biomass (largely informal). For Egypt the dataset’s own retail prices imply exactly this: rp = (sp + txo) x 1.14 for residential gas and the oil products, and rp = sp + txo for power and industry. So historical oil-product retail prices equal the dataset’s (14% higher than without the rule), and new policies pay 14% VAT in those sectors.

title: 4  Prices and energy demand
text:
1. Dimensions and units

Prices are kept by fuel x price sector, as in the IMF dataset: 12 price fuels, namely coal and natural gas for power, residential and industry; gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, other oil products and biomass for all sectors. Electricity is left to the power module. Subsectors take the price of their price sector (road and residential use the residential coal and gas prices).
All in real $/GJ of the results year (A1-A3).

title: 4  Prices and energy demand
text:
2. International prices gp
gp_t = international price of the source and commodity x deflator x adjustment factor.

Source: ScenarioDefinition IntEnerPricForeSource, asterisk dropped (IMF-WB* = average of IMF and WB).
Commodity: crude oil (gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, other oil products); coal; gas of the country’s market (Egypt Global = average of LNG, North America and Europe); a flat 1 (biomass).
Factor (ScenarioDefinition IntEnerPricForecastAdjustment): Base = 1; High / Low = 1.5 / 0.5 for oil and 1.25 / 0.75 for gas and coal, after the last historical year.

title: 4  Prices and energy demand
text:
3. Supply cost sp
Data up to the last historical year L; then sp_t = fixsp + (sp_{t-1} - fixsp - ps_{t-1}) x gp_t / gp_{t-1} + ps_t: a fixed part, a part that floats with the international price, and the existing producer subsidy ps (block row psp, $/GJ; legacy sp = fixsp + fltsp + ps, rows 2455-2708; v0.6.1, I49). The producer subsidy phase-out is not in sp: it is a separate new-policy wedge (section 6b; v0.6.2).
fixsp = (margin + bucketed pass-through x production cost [coal, gas]) x CPI index(2022) / GJ per unit. The margin of biomass is 0 (legacy hardcode; other oil products from data, A10). Producer subsidies enter through ps (section 6b; 0 for Egypt).

title: 4  Prices and energy demand
text:
4. Excise and other taxes txo (pass-through)

Pass-through pcc: raw = the dataset’s base-year value (blank = 0; biomass = 1; other oil products from data, A10). Bucketed: <= 0.25 -> 0, <= 0.5 -> 0.5, else 1. Settings GovPriceControls chooses Bucketed (default), Manual or None = 1. Manual takes the retail price control (pass-through) of the block from sheet Manual inputs J167:J180, the legacy addresses, by the code in column G (mit.rp.<fuel>.<sector>.ctrl; legacy default 0.8 for every block); a blank cell gives 1, as legacy rows 747-760. The electricity rows (J178:J179) are not read: electricity prices come from the power section. Egypt bucketed: coal 1, gas 0, oil products incl. other oil products 0, biomass 1.
Historical txo (as legacy): coal, gas and biomass rp / (1 + vr) - sp; oil products the dataset’s txo (legacy builds their retail price as sp + txo, times (1 + vr)).
Projected: txo_t = txo_L x pcc + cs_t, with the floating subsidy cs_t = (sp_L - sp_t + txo_L(1 - pcc)) x (1 - pcc), and cs_t not below txo_L(1 - pcc) when that is >= 0.
pcc = 1: supply-cost changes are passed on in full. pcc = 0: the retail price before new policies stays at its value in L, and the floating subsidy absorbs the change.

title: 4  Prices and energy demand
section: 5. Retail price before new policies rpb and the after-tax price atp
text:
5. Retail price before new policies rpb and the after-tax price atp
rpb = (sp + txo) x (1 + vr), with vr the VAT rate of L (A11). For gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene vr is the VAT rate x the household share of the product (sheet OilProductShares; Egypt: gasoline 1, diesel 0.03, LPG 0.99, kerosene 0.39), as legacy rows 797-816: VAT is charged on the household part only, firms reclaim it (v0.4.12, LD5; issue I39). Other oil products and the other fuels take the full rate, as legacy.
By subsector: atp = max(rpb + (nce + xcpd) x (1 + vr), 0.01). New policies (nce = new carbon tax + new ETS cost + new excise) are passed through in full and pay VAT (legacy vat = (sp + txo) x vr with nce inside txo); xcpd is the change in existing carbon pricing (section 5b). The 0.01 floor is legacy’s.
Residential LPG and kerosene always exempted (ScenarioDefinition AlwaysExemptResLPGKer, row 268, by scenario; default No; legacy rows 5546-5547). If the switch starts with “Yes” (Yes or Yes), the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise of the residential LPG and kerosene rows are 0: each is multiplied by the exemption factor of Section-1 rows exf (exf.all = 1, exf.res = 0 if Yes), at the row’s position in Inputs column exg (2 for residential LPG and kerosene, 1 elsewhere). Their nce is then 0, so atp = max(rpb + (xcpd + csw + pcw) x (1 + vr), 0.01): no new policy and no VAT on it, while existing taxes, the change in existing carbon pricing and the subsidy phase-outs stay, as legacy (row 2651, the price before new policies). The shadow price shp is not exempted, as legacy. The new-policy revenue of these rows (rnew, the excise revenue rex and the VAT on the new policies in rvt) is 0 with the price. ETS-covered emissions still count them where the residential sector is in an ETS. The residential leakage to biomass reads the row’s own nce, so an exempt fuel does not leak (Equations.md 4a).

Layout of a price block and the price incl. new policies by block
Each fuel | sector block of section 2 reads: settings (italic: parameter row, international reference price gpi, fixed supply cost spf, existing subsidy per price unit esubpu); the full retail price rpn (bold); the build-up sp, txf, txo, etx, esub, vat ending with rpb; then the new taxes and subsidies.
New policies act by subsector (sections 5-8). The block shows them as averages over the subsectors priced by the block (the atp rows whose D is the block position), weighted by their fuel use ener:

pnq = sum of ener over those subsectors (ktoe);
pctx, pets, pntx, pxcd = fuel-use weighted averages of ctxnew, ets, ntx, xcpd;
rpn = sum(atp x ener) / pnq (rpb where pnq = 0);
pnce = rpn - rpb, the total new policy; pvatn = pnce - (pctx + pets + pntx + pxcd), the VAT on the new policies (and the 0.01 floor).

These are weighted averages with each scenario’s own quantities, not price indices; price changes between scenarios are the indices of section 7.

5b. Existing carbon pricing
Legacy CPAT adds existing carbon taxes and ETS from its sheet ECP (WB Carbon Pricing Dashboard, ICAP; as of 1 April 2025) as parts of txo (Mitigation rows 1675-1764). Since v0.4.12 the prototype follows legacy with several schemes (user decision 2026-10-18; was issue I7), with legacy bugs L61-L65 fixed. It differs in how the level enters: the IMF retail prices already contain whatever existing carbon pricing a country had, so only the change against that level enters (below); legacy subtracts the same level from the fixed part of txo, which gives the same numbers.

Data (sheet ECP at its legacy addresses, 52 countries; Egypt has none). Each code is looked up in its own legacy block (sheet Inputs_ecp, columns K:L give the block’s first and last row):

carbon tax: single rate ecr.all, fuel rates ecr.<fuel>, sector coverage ecs.<sector>, fuel coverage ecf.<fuel> (rows 69-559);
national ETS: price eer.all, coverage ees, eef (rows 600-615, 619-737, 1040-1093);
regional EU ETS: the EU price (row 616) and the country’s regional coverage (rows 738-1036, 1094-1223), where the country’s “EU ETS?” flag (general information, column K) is Yes or Both (legacy row 1695).

Prices in real USD of ResultsYear (nominal x CPI index). Coverage of each data year (2021-2025; blank = 0, as legacy), the last data year after.
Carbon tax rate by fuel (legacy rows 1752-1764): the fuel rate where the country has one and no “single price” flag (general information, column E), else the single rate.
Sector of a price: the ECP sector of the price fuel, as legacy: coal and gas by their price sector (power, residential, industry); oil products, biomass and jet fuel transport; other oil products industry (power: power).
Tables (sheet Inputs_ecp), by ECP sector | fuel and data year, $/tCO2: carbon tax = rate x sector coverage x fuel coverage; ETS = national price x its coverage + EU price x the regional coverage (the two schemes add up, as legacy).
Scenario factors (section 1, ScenarioDefinition): xct.p = 1 if ExistingCTApply = Yes, x (1 + ExistingCTGrowth)^(years after the last data year), else 0; xets.p the same with ExistingETSApply, ExistingETSGrowth (legacy grows the EU ETS with the carbon-tax growth: bug L61). xct.c is the data column of the year.
Per subsector and fuel: level xcp = EF x (carbon tax x xct.p + ETS x xets.p) ($/GJ); change xcpd = the level minus the level embedded in the price data (xcp0, Inputs: the tables in the last historical price year L). Only the change enters the after-tax price, so a country’s history is not counted twice: switching a scheme off lowers the price by its embedded level; growth or new data raise it.
Power: the same change per kWh (row pow | fuel of the tables) is part of the variable cost before new policies, so dispatch, investment and electricity prices respond.
New carbon tax: if CTaxComplimentaryToETS = Yes (legacy rows 2270-2288), it covers 1 - the national ETS sector coverage of the year (legacy: of the previous year, bug L65). Otherwise new instruments add to existing ones.
Revenue: existing-tax revenue includes xcpd x (1 + vr); a memo shows the level, fuel use x xcp. Existing ETS revenue is valued at the full permit price, as legacy; legacy’s free-allocation and revenue data (ECP rows 560-597, 1225-1322) are not used in legacy’s model either.
Legacy bugs fixed (register): L61 (EU ETS growth), L62 (transport diesel, LPG and kerosene take the rate row as coverage), L63 (fuel coverage lookup stops at row 403 of a block that ends at 425), L64 (no ETS on other oil products outside power), L65 (complementary tax with last year’s coverage).

section: 6b. Subsidy and price-control phase-outs, producer subsidies (v0.4.16; LD18, LD19)
text:
6b. Subsidy and price-control phase-outs, producer subsidies (v0.4.16; LD18, LD19)
User decision 2026-10-18: separate policy lines by sector and fuel, not meshed with the pre-policy price build-up. sp, txo and rpb are unchanged; the reforms are wedges added to the after-tax price, like the new policies.

Factors (section 1, legacy rows 2211-2218). One per phase-out: producer subsidies (ScenarioDefinition 123-129), consumer subsidies (131-137) and price controls (191-195). Scenario 1 reads the baseline switch, period and share; other scenarios the policy switch and period, with share = MAX(baseline, policy) (legacy rows 264-274). The price-control phase-out applies if its switch is on and the scenario is a policy scenario or its baseline switch is on, and it takes the consumer share (as legacy: issue I48). Factor pof = MAX(1 - share, 1 - share x (year - start) / period after the start year): the share of the original kept, the same year for every line (legacy lags the fixed subsidy a year: bug L81).
Lines by price fuel | sector. csf.<block> = 1 - csi x (1 - factor), pcf.<block> likewise with pci; the inclusion switches csi, pci (sheet Constants, default 1 for every block, as legacy) let a reform cover some fuels and sectors only. Producer subsidies by fuel (coal, gas, oil, biomass, electricity): psi, psf.
Split of txo (each price block). Fixed part txfx = pass-through x txo (history: of the year; projection: of the last historical year); floating part txfl = txo - txfx (it absorbs the supply-cost changes not passed through). As legacy rows 2597-2599.
Wedges (each block, $/GJ before VAT). Consumer subsidy reform pcsw = -(1 - csf) x MIN(txfx, 0): only a fixed subsidy goes (legacy: the fixed subsidy x factor). Price-control phase-out ppcw = -(1 - pcf) x txfl: the floating part goes, subsidy or tax (legacy row 2599). For Egypt every subsidised fuel has pass-through 0, so only the price-control phase-out removes subsidies, as in legacy.
Subsectors. csw, pcw = the wedges of the subsector’s block; atp = MAX(rpb + (nce + xcpd + csw + pcw) x (1 + vr), floor). Revenue rsr = fuel use x PJ/ktoe x (csw + pcw) x (1 + vr): the subsidy saved plus VAT on it (section 12; 12e books it under existing taxes and subsidies, its VAT under VAT). rnet stays the pre-reform existing revenue.
Producer subsidies (fiscal line). pros.<fuel> = Prices_dom mit.pros.<fuel>.all (USD bn nominal) x CPI factor, held after the last price year; rpsu.all = -SUMPRODUCT(pros, psf) in section 12 (negative = cost), in the total revenue and the fiscal space; 12e producer subsidies = the electricity subsidy gap + rpsu. Price effect (v0.6.1, I49, as legacy rows 825-829): section-1 rows psd.<fuel> hold the demand that carries the subsidy: oil, world demand x liters per ktoe (legacy _conv_ktoe_liter_oil = 1,108,792); coal and gas, the average of world demand and domestic consumption (EnergyCons, excluding electricity and heat) x GJ per ktoe; biomass, domestic consumption x GJ per ktoe. psu.<fuel> = -pros x USDperM / psd up to the last price year, then held: the existing subsidy. Each price block reads the psu of its fuel by its international price position (G) into psp ($/GJ: x liters per barrel for other oil products, / GJ per price unit), which stays in the supply cost and so in the price before new policies rpb.

Producer subsidy reform (v0.6.2, user rule 2026-10-20: subsidy reforms are always separate from the before-tax build-up). psr.<fuel> = -psu x (1 - psf) (legacy: the base value x the phase-out factor, row 2213). The block wedge ppsw = psr of its fuel ($/GJ as psp) x the block’s pass-through pcc, beside the consumer subsidy and price-control wedges pcsw and ppcw; the subsectors read it as psw into the after-tax price (atp = rpb + (new taxes + xcpd + csw + pcw + psw) x (1 + VAT)), and the VAT on it is in the subsidy-reform revenue rsr. Legacy puts the phase-out into the supply cost, where the price controls absorb (1 - pcc) of it; the wedge x pcc gives the same price except where the excise floor binds. Legacy bugs fixed: L124 (residential gas read the oil value) and L125 (other oil products added a per-liter value to a per-barrel price). Egypt: no producer subsidy data (0). - Not yet: electricity consumer subsidy phase-out (PowerSubsidyExemptInclude, default DoNotPhaseOut) and the electricity producer subsidy in the power price: with the power features (legacy bugs L83, L84 to fix then).

title: 5  Power
text:
Power engineer model: method
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Power.md.
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
Scope. The quantity side of the power sector: power demand (legacy table H), dispatch (I), capacity and retirement (K), investment (L), and the cost rows investment needs: shadow price and rebate (D6), levelised variable cost (D9) and levelised investment cost (E1). The price side is in chapter Power. The legacy reference is Mitigation section 4 of CPAT 1.0pre_456_NoPropData.xlsb: rows 2954-4297 for the baseline, rows 9285-10628 for the carbon-tax run.
Inputs by scenario. Every ScenarioDefinition power input is read in the scenario’s own ScenarioDefinition column (section 1, “Power sector settings”: rows 242, 262, 342-415 and 482), as legacy runs each column with its own runs. Sub-table A0 of section 3 applies them to the power data of the country (Inputs): capacity factor, efficiency, WACC and discounted lifetime, fuel per kWh, base-year capacity, new investment permitted and its start year, scale-up and retirement rates, the early-retirement factor, the capex decline scenario, storage, PPA, renewable subsidy, rebate and excise settings. Scenario 1 is the baseline of every scenario, so a technical input (logit constants, WACC, capacity-factor bounds, storage, cost decline) changed in a policy scenario changes that scenario only, and its difference to scenario 1 mixes the input change with the policy; technical inputs are not usually changed across scenarios. Not read (no prototype feature): CostBreakdownYear, ElasticityModel, PowGenCostsOldNew, UseElasticityModelPowerDemandInEngineerModel, SupplyCostDeltaSubsidy, the coal implicit cost (369-371). The final deficit to gas is a global switch (Settings C45, PwDeficitGas), as legacy’s typed cell.
Alignment. The prototype follows legacy formula by formula, except for ten bugs, which are fixed; Legacy_CPAT_Bugs_v<version>.docx lists them with their effects. power_model_ref.py implements the method in Python with one switch per bug; with all switches off it reproduces 208 cached legacy rows of both runs to 1e-13. Planned retirement is available for every generation type; legacy offers it for coal only.
Links with the rest of the model. Power demand follows its own elasticities (H). Sector policies (carbon tax, ETS, feebates, fuel price reform) act on the fuel blocks only, not on power demand; electricity demand by sector is a memo, not part of the fuel totals, so nothing is counted twice. Power CO2 enters the CO2 totals (by fuel and as ETS sector power, so a new ETS covering power sees it, and the baseline CO2 data include it). Generation fuel use of coal, gas, oil and biomass enters total fuel use; nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables have no fuel. Power revenues enter the revenue totals: fuel taxes and subsidies on generation, the change in existing carbon pricing, electricity VAT and subsidy gap, and new policies with the ETS at the permit price. Existing carbon pricing changes the variable cost before new policies (chapter Prices section 5b). A Settings switch turns the legacy 2023-2024 demand shock on (default off, as for fuels).
Units: generation and capacity in MW / MWy; demand in ktoe; costs in real $/kWh of 2026.

title: 5  Power
text:
1. Order within a year and across years
year t:  H  demand(t)        <- demand(t-1), GDP(t), price(t-1)              (no circularity: price lagged)
         K1 capacity(t)      <- capacity(t-1) - retirement(t-1) + investment(t-1)
         I  dispatch(t)      <- capacity(t), required generation(t), variable costs(t)
            shares(t)        -> J VRE share -> storage cost(t) -> B (vintages), C (levelised)
            shares(t)        -> E average generation cost(t) -> G supply cost(t+1) -> price(t+1) -> demand(t+2)
         K  retirement(t)    <- capacity(t), early coal retirement (coal variable cost vs wind and solar costs)
         L  investment(t)    <- required generation(t) - capacity after retirement(t); logit on E1(t)
                             -> capacity(t+1); share in the stock phi(t) -> B vintages(t+1)
The levelised variable cost D9(t) averages the variable cost from t to the end of the horizon. Variable costs depend only on prices and policies, not on the generation mix, so D9 is computed before the year loop, backwards from the last year.


2. Method (with fixes)
H Demand. Four demand groups (transport, residential, industry, services), with electricity elasticities to income, usage, efficiency and autonomous efficiency (eps_Y, eps_U, eps_F, alpha). - Each group’s price is last year’s residential and industrial prices weighted 0.5/0.5 for transport, 1/0 for residential, 0/1 for industry and services. - Each group’s demand multiple combines autonomous efficiency, GDP growth (with the income factor), the price change and an optional shock: (1 / (1 + alpha + extra))^(1 + eps_U) × (1 + GDP growth)^(eps_Y × inc) × (price ratio)^(eps_U + eps_F + eps_U eps_F) × (1 + shock × switch). - Demand of each of the 15 subsectors = last year’s × its group’s multiple (services use the services multiple in every year). - Required generation (MWy) = demand × (1 + net exports + transmission + own use + statistical difference shares), converted from ktoe. In the base year it is actual generation. - Memo: demand by group, and electricity demand by subsector, sector and in total.
A0 Data of the scenario. - Capacity factor = actual (base-year output / installed capacity) when strictly between the CFOverride bounds of the scenario (wind and solar: CFOverrideIfBelowWndSol; others: CFOverrideIfBelowFosOth; upper CFOverrideIfAbove), else the studies value. Efficiency = actual (output / input) unless below MinimumThermalEfficiency (or without input), else the studies value. - WACC: Country* (country WACC + coal premium), Tech (country WACC + technology premium), else MAX(WACCUserGlobal (User), the income-group WACC (Income) or the studies WACC, MinimumWACC). Discounted lifetime = (1 − (1 + WACC)^−N) / (1 − (1 + WACC)^−1); renewables use the average of wind and solar. - New investment: the type’s NewInv setting; “If Present” = Yes when the type has more than 0.1% of base-year capacity; from the NewInv year (hydro from the base year when its generation share is above one half). - Scale-up rates: coal, gas, hydro MaxNonVREAsPCOfTotalGen; wind and solar the country default (CtryDefault), MaxWindSolarScaleup (UserDefined) or the category rate (Low, Medium, High, Vhigh); the others MaxNonNucOreBioAsPCOfTotalGen. Retirement rate 1/N, hydro 0 if HydroDoesntRetire = Yes. - Capex time factors of the decline scenario of RenewableCostDeclineRate (renewables; others medium); where the Power tab has no series for the option (Low and Vhigh for wind and solar, Vhigh for other renewables), the older series of the same option, else medium.
I Dispatch. - Fixed-output types (wind, solar, hydro, other renewables, oil, nuclear, biomass) generate capacity × capacity factor. - Coal and gas cover the rest. Each first gets the minimum it must supply given the other’s maximum (maximum = capacity × MaximumCoalCF for coal, × MaximumGasCF for gas; 0.9 by default); the remainder is shared by a logit EXP(-kDispatch × variable cost / lowest variable cost), capped at the maximum. - PPAs: a share p of coal and gas generation (PPAProportionCoalGas × phase-out factor) runs at its capacity factor, scaled to the need, whatever its cost: generation = logit dispatch × (1 − p) + effective capacity × (coal and gas need / coal and gas effective capacity) × p. The phase-out factor falls linearly to 0 over YearsToPhaseOutPPAs years after YearPPACoalGas when the switch of the scenario (PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsBaseline in scenario 1, PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsPolicy in the others) is Yes or Yes*; else 1. - Fuel use = generation / efficiency (ktoe); CO2 = fuel use × EF.
K Capacity and retirement. - Retirement = planned retirement (data in nameplate MW per year, if the type’s switch is Yes) or else capacity / lifetime; plus early retirement for coal; at most the capacity. Hydro does not retire. Effective retirement = retirement × capacity factor. - For Egypt the legacy file has no planned-retirement data, so every switch is No. - Early coal retirement: room = MAX(0, maximum wind and solar additions − last year’s increase in generation − last year’s non-coal effective retirements); early = MAX(0, MIN(0.8 × coal effective capacity, room) × (1 − coal share of a logit over coal variable cost and wind and solar investment costs)) / coal capacity factor × factor × (1 − PPA share). The factor is MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement, and 0 in scenario 1 unless EarlyRetirementInBaseline = Yes (legacy F3993); plants under PPA do not retire early. - Capacity needed = MAX(required generation − (effective capacity − effective retirement), 0). Capacity bought in year t is available in t+1.
L Investment. - First round, permitted types only: logit share EXP(-2 × E1 / lowest permitted E1), limited by a scale-up limit (rate × total effective capacity). - Second round: the remaining deficit goes to types with space left, cheapest first. - Final deficit: with PwDeficitGas = Yes (Settings C45; default No, as legacy’s typed switch E4248) the deficit left after the second round goes to gas (legacy row 4252). - Nameplate investment = effective / capacity factor; USD = nameplate × capital cost of the year. - phi = nameplate / (capacity + nameplate − retirement), the new-vintage share used in the vintage averages B2 and B6.
D5, D6, D9, E1. Each sector has three policy rates ($/tCO2), the same for the fuel blocks and power: - carbon tax = carbon price × sector coverage × (1 − ETS coverage); - ETS cost = ETS tax-equivalent price × ETS coverage × (1 − OBR share); - shadow price = feebate (and regulation) rate × share impacting efficiency + ETS tax-equivalent price × ETS coverage × OBR share.
New policy cost per kWh (D5) = tCO2/kWh × (carbon tax × fuel coverage + ETS cost) + fuel price reform per kWh. The levelised fixed cost (C) includes the renewable subsidy per kWh of the scenario (chapter Power 3.3). The shadow price per kWh is the power shadow price × tCO2/kWh; the rebate returns it in proportion to base-year shares, per kWh generated. Total variable cost = cost before new policies + new policy cost + shadow price + rebate. D9 = discounted average of the total variable cost to 2041, the last year (as legacy). E1 = MAX(levelised fixed cost + D9, 0.01).


3. Validation (check_report_v0.6.4.md)

Method = legacy. The Python reference, fed with the cached legacy inputs and the bugs switched on, reproduces 208 legacy rows of the baseline and the carbon-tax run.
Workbook = Python. With all bugs fixed and the prototype inputs, the workbook matches the Python reference for every power row, in every scenario test.
Properties: generation = required generation; the capacity balance holds; investment is at most the capacity needed (scale-up limits can leave part unplaced); the supply cost lag holds; a carbon price raises the VRE share and lowers power CO2.
Planned retirement. With the switch on for gas and oil and test data, the workbook matches the Python reference, and retirement equals the data. 4b. Power features. One test scenario per feature (check section 5d): MaximumGasCF and long-term storage; the power inputs of the scenario (two scenarios with many inputs changed, including WACC options, capacity-factor and efficiency bounds, permits, scale-up categories, decline options, storage, logit constants, pass-through, spot prices); PPAs; renewable subsidies; the rebate; the electricity excise and the manual excise; the final deficit to gas with tight scale-up limits. Each matches the Python reference.
Memo lines equal power demand by subsector and add up by sector and in total.
Totals. Fuel use, revenue and CO2 totals with power equal the Python reference; with non-zero existing carbon pricing test data, the power variable cost, revenues by type and totals match too. Check rows confirm that the totals equal their sector, power and fuel parts.



Manual capacity and investment (v0.5.6, power plan P3)
Where a scenario’s NewInv = Manual (ScenarioDefinition rows 397-405), the type follows the capacity path of ‘Manual inputs’ (rows 349-357 for scenario 1, rows 363-371 for the other scenarios; names ManCapVal, ManCapYr). Row mancap reads the path; row mani is the manual new effective investment, MAX(0, next year’s path - this year’s path + retirement) x capacity factor (0 in 2041); the type gets no logit investment (permit 0). Row needm = MAX(need - SUM(mani), 0) sizes the logit and second-round investment: legacy computes this need (row 4108) but never uses it, so its logit investment comes on top of the manual one (legacy bug L118, fixed). New effective investment nei = first + second (+ gas deficit) + mani. Test (scenario 2, nuclear 2,400 MW from 2030): 2,400 MW nameplate built in 2029, then the retirements replaced.


Coal implicit cost (v0.5.6, power plan P5)
Rows cics, cicl and cic (sub-table D): AdditionalCoalIntangibleCost (ScenarioDefinition 369) No = 0, Manual = ScenarioDefinition 370-371, else the GoalSeekCoal table (legacy tab, 85 countries, not Egypt) by country; linear from the first year of calculations to CoalICYr (2030), as legacy rows 3360-3363. It is added to the coal variable cost (dispatch, levelised cost, investment) and, unless Settings PwCoalICTariff = No (default Yes, as legacy; decision 6), to the generation cost and tariffs. title: 5  Power
section: Power generation costs and power prices: method
text:
Power generation costs and power prices: method
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
Scope. The price side of the power sector: - what each generation type costs per kWh; - what the generation mix costs on average; - the end-user electricity prices for residential and industrial users; - the power-sector carbon cost and its revenue, by user group and by generation type, and the power part of the revenue totals.
It follows legacy CPAT section 4 (“Technoeconomic (‘engineer’) power model”, Mitigation rows 2954-3672 and 3867-3927) and documentation chapter 3, sections 3.4.1 and 3.4.2.5, keeping legacy’s sub-table letters (A Inputs, B Amortised costs, C Levelised costs, D Variable costs, E Total costs, F Memos, G End-user prices, J Storage, plus M Revenues by type). The quantities (demand H, dispatch I, capacity K, investment L) come from the engineer model (chapter Power): generation shares, investment shares and consumption. A policy scenario’s power prices therefore respond to its own generation mix, investment and demand.
Units: real US dollars of the results year (2026) per kWh, unless stated. Every ScenarioDefinition power setting (pass-through, minimum cost, storage, WACC, capacity factor and efficiency bounds, renewable subsidy, rebate, excise) is read in the scenario’s own ScenarioDefinition column (chapter Power, inputs by scenario). Generation types f: coal, natural gas, oil, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro, other renewables, biomass (legacy order).

1. Interactions
The price block is mostly a one-way chain. The table lists its links with the rest of the model and how legacy keeps them free of circular references; the prototype implements all of them.

Two consequences shape the design: 1. End-user prices depend on generation costs only through the weighted average (E) and the transmission add-on. Variable, amortised and storage costs matter for prices only as far as they enter that average. 2. The renewables systems cost is an interaction inside the price block. The VRE share sets the marginal storage cost (J), which enters the cost of wind and solar in two ways: amortised, through vintages, in the cost of the existing stock (B), which goes into end-user prices; and levelised, in the cost of new plants (C), which goes into investment. So a scenario that adds renewables raises their storage cost per kWh, which feeds back into the average generation cost a year later.


2. Simplifications against legacy

3. Method by legacy sub-table

3.1 A. Inputs (one row of constants per generation type, and a few year paths)

3.2 B. Amortised (cost-recovery) fixed costs: the cost of the existing stock

Weighted average capex of the stock: last year’s average and last year’s new capex, weighted by last year’s Φ; in the base year, the base-year capex. Exact match with legacy.
Weighted average storage cost of vintages: the same, but new vintages take the current-year marginal storage cost. Exact match with legacy.
Amortised fixed cost (S1) = (average capex × (1/N + wacc/2) + dtc/N) / (cf × 8,760) + average storage cost + opf.



3.3 C. Levelised (forward-looking) fixed costs: new plants (investment)
Levelised fixed cost (S2) = (cax + dtc + tcx) / (cf × 8,760 × dlf) + marginal storage cost + opf + rns.


3.3b Renewable subsidies (A17, C5)

Subsidy per kWh rns(t) = −(base subsidy RenewableSubsidyBL + additional subsidy RenSubsidyAddUSDkwh × MAX(0, 1 − (t − start)/n) from the start year RenSubsidyAddStartYear, policy scenarios only), with n = RenSubsidyAddPhaseoutYrs. The inputs are labelled nominal and used as real, as legacy.
It applies to wind, solar, other renewables and biomass, and to hydro if RenewableSubsidyHydro = Yes.
It enters the levelised fixed cost (investment), not the cost of the existing stock or the end-user price; its revenue is rns × generation by type (negative), in the power subsidies and in row ren of the revenue by policy.



3.4 D. Current variable costs

Fuel price for power (A18; v0.6.2, legacy bug L126): average of the fuel price before new policies fpn over t-4 .. t from the base year (one year in 2022, five from 2026); legacy averages t-2 .. t+2, which reads later years. The spot price is a switch. Row fpn holds this year’s price, so the average reads one row and only the scenario’s own years.
Fuel cost per kWh = fuel price × 0.0036 / ν. Nuclear: 0.004 $/kWh. Renewables 0.
Change in existing carbon pricing against the price data (chapter Prices section 5b): tCO2/kWh × the change in the existing carbon tax and ETS price, weighted by their coverage of power and the fuel (0 for Egypt).
Variable cost before new policies = variable O&M + fuel cost + change in existing carbon pricing.
Carbon cost per kWh generated = the new policy wedge on the fuel in power ($/GJ) × 0.0036 / ν. The wedge sums the carbon tax (carbon price × EF × fuel coverage × power coverage × (1 − ETS coverage of power)), the ETS (tax-equivalent price × EF × ETS coverage of power × (1 − OBR share of power)) and the fuel price reform for coal and gas in power.
Total variable cost = cost before new policies + carbon cost + shadow price + rebate (feebates and the output-based part of the ETS). Dispatch uses it.



3.5 E. Total costs

Generation cost before carbon (cost recovery, legacy E3) = amortised fixed cost + variable cost before new policies.
Average generation cost = generation-share-weighted average of that cost.
Average carbon cost per kWh consumed = share-weighted carbon cost × generation / consumption. The ratio covers losses, own use and net exports, from the base-year balance.

Carbon is kept out of the average generation cost and added separately (legacy, documentation 3.4.1.7), so a rebate can be computed against it.


3.6 F. Memos
F7 switching carbon prices, F1 system cost and F4 carbon intensity are memos. Only F4 (tCO2 per kWh = EF × 0.0036/ν) is built, as a parameter.


3.7 J. Systems integration cost of renewables (storage)

VRE share v = share of wind + solar + other renewables (legacy row 3851).
Short-term storage (batteries): marginal hours = ast × 18 × v, with ast = 1 the share allocated to VRE and 18 = d(9 v²)/dv. Cost per hour per kWh = (battery capex + interface capex / 2 hours kWh/kW) / (dlf of renewables × 8,760) + battery opex / 8,760.
Long-term storage (electrolysers): marginal units = LongTermStorageFor100pcVRE × 2 × max(0, v − x) / (1 − x)², with x = StartingPointWhenLTStorageIsNeeded (0.75). Cost per unit = (electrolyser capex + LT storage capex per kWh × StorageHoursForLTStorage) / (dlf of renewables × 8,760) + fixed opex / 8,760 + variable opex.
Marginal storage cost of wind, solar and other renewables = hours × cost per hour + units × cost per unit; 0 for other types.

Legacy has a 33% “allocation of LT storage to VRE” parameter and applies it twice (rows 3911 and 3912, a bug). The prototype applies it once.


3.8 G. End-user prices (residential and industrial)

Supply cost (I5, lagged) = last year’s average generation cost + transmission (0.040 $/kWh residential, 0.015 industrial). In the base year, the base-year average cost.
Price before new policies (S4): up to the last historical year L, the historical retail price including VAT from the price dataset (nominal → real with the CPI index); after L, last year’s value + pass-through × change in supply cost × (1 + VAT of L), with pass-through 1 (legacy hardcode).
End-user price = price before new policies + (average carbon cost × pass-through × (1 − rebate switch) + excise) × (1 + VAT). As in legacy (rows 3614-3617), VAT is charged on the new policy terms.
Rebate switch (legacy rows 261, 2188, J3595): 1 in policy scenarios with PowerRebates = Yes (or Yes*) or a feebate scenario of the legacy scenario table (Feebates, Power Supply Feebates, Power feebate); the carbon cost is then not passed to electricity users.
Excise per kWh before VAT = electricity excise + pass-through × (manual excise − its value in the last historical year) after that year. The electricity excise (scenario Electricity excise, policy scenarios; legacy row 2253) = grid CO2 intensity of the base year (CO2 of the fuel input to power / power output, Balances) × carbon price. The manual excise (policy scenarios with AdditionalExcise = Yes; legacy rows 3602, 3631) is the new electricity excise of ‘Manual inputs’ rows 161-162 (real, or nominal × the deflator index if NomorReal is not Real); like legacy it enters the price before policy, so up to the last historical year it is absorbed by the price data and later its change is passed through.
Subsidy gap (S7) = price before new policies / (1 + VAT) − supply cost. Negative = price below the modelled supply cost (subsidies are negative).



3.9 G4 and M. Revenues (USD million real) and the revenue totals
By user group (G), each × consumption of the group: - VAT = price before new policies × VAT / (1 + VAT); - VAT on the new-policy cost passed through = (average carbon cost × pass-through × (1 − rebate switch) + excise) × VAT; - rebate (negative) = − rebate switch × average carbon cost × pass-through: the carbon cost returned to users (the VAT on it is not collected); - excise = excise per kWh × consumption, of which the electricity excise of the scenario (carbon-based) and the manual excise; - subsidy gap (signed: negative = fiscal cost, positive when the price is above the modelled supply cost); - new-policy cost (memo; it values the ETS at the tax-equivalent price) = average carbon cost.
By generation type (M), with a fuel flag of 1 for coal, gas, oil and biomass: - existing taxes on generation fuels = flag × fuel use × (excise + VAT) of the price fuel; - existing subsidies on generation fuels = flag × fuel use × subsidy (negative); - change in existing carbon pricing × generation; - new policies = generation × carbon cost − CO2 × the power ETS cost rate × (1 − revenue factor): the ETS part at the permit price, as in the subsectors; - existing carbon pricing level (memo) = CO2 × the covered existing carbon tax and ETS prices.
The revenue totals add a power row: existing taxes = fuel taxes + change in existing carbon pricing + electricity VAT; subsidies = fuel subsidies + subsidy gap + renewable subsidies; new policies = new-policy revenue by type + VAT on new policies + rebate + excise; existing carbon pricing level = the memo by type. In the revenue by policy (12e), the rebate and the carbon-based excise count with the carbon tax, the manual excise with the excise, and the renewable subsidies in their own row (as legacy rows 7749, 7762, 7903, the base subsidy once). The fuel subsidy and the subsidy gap do not overlap: the supply cost already uses the subsidised fuel price, so the gap is what remains between that cost and the tariff.



4. Validation

Method = legacy. A Python reference feeds the legacy inputs (its fuel prices, shares, Φ, prices and VAT) into this method and reproduces the cached legacy rows B2, B6, B8, C7, D4, E3, the weighted average, J storage, and G1/G2 supply cost and prices, to a relative error below 1e-6.
Workbook = Python for the prototype’s own inputs (corrected Egypt prices, moving-average fuel prices as legacy), as for the other checks.
Formula uniformity and copies of scenario groups, as for the rest of the sheet.
Regression against the previous version (shared output codes). The power block feeds total fuel use (generation fuel use), revenues and CO2.

Result at the first build of the price block (check_report_v0.1.05.md, PASS): 80 legacy rows reproduced, largest relative difference 5.6e-17; all 28 power variables equal the Python reference in every scenario test, largest relative difference about 5e-15; one formula per block; 3,642 codes unchanged against the previous version.


5. Decisions

Fuel prices for power: moving average as legacy (user decision); spot prices remain a switch (S5).
VAT on power policy terms: legacy charges VAT (row 3614); the prototype does too, as for fuels.
Historical electricity prices: the corrected Egypt block (residential 0.054, 0.048, 0.043 $/kWh nominal, 2022-2024) differs from legacy’s vintage (0.097 in 2022). The prototype uses the corrected block.
Producer-side subsidy data: the corrected block has none for electricity; legacy used −9.2 bn USD in 2022. The prototype reports the modelled subsidy gap instead (S7).



v0.5.6: fuel price reform, price floor, renewable subsidies in real terms

The electricity fuel price reform path of the scenario (section-1 rows fpr.ecy.res, fpr.ecy.ind; ScenarioDefinition 148-149, 162-163) enters the manual excise of policy scenarios (row entx), as legacy row 216 (issue I59, replicated).
End-user electricity prices are floored at MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice (row rp), as legacy rows 3617 and 3646 (issue I60, replicated; 0.01 $/kWh: not binding for Egypt).
The renewable subsidy inputs (ScenarioDefinition 354-355, labelled nominal) are converted to real with the CPI factor of the year (row rnsp; legacy bug L114, fixed).
The levelised cost includes TransmissionCostShare (ScenarioDefinition appendix block B, default 1) of the transmission capex (legacy IncludeTransmissionCostsInGenerationCostsPercent).

8. Legacy bugs and oddities in these chains

A2 rows 2981–2985 (wnd, sol, hyd, ore, bio), columns P..T: the IF(ISERROR(INDEX(K)),INDEX(K),IF(ISERROR(INDEX(L)),INDEX(L),INDEX(M))) logic is inverted, so the result is always the world value. Country efficiency, fixed opex, variable opex, WACC and lifetime for these techs are ignored. Egypt: solar fixed opex uses 15 instead of the country 11.831, which changes opf|sol.
A4 column N (installed capacity): the column range Power!$F$357:$Y$357 (2000–2019) does not contain FirstYearCalculations (2022, column AB), so N = #N/A. Actual capacity factors are never used; CF = study values, and the CFOverride bounds are dead.
Hydro investment start (H4067): IF($L$3827>50%, …) tests a year header (2022 > 0.5), so hydro always starts in the first year (2022 instead of NewInvHydYear = 2030).
Regional/country code shadowing: MATCH over Power!A25:A356 finds the regional rows (42–109) first for chn.mpp.*, jpn.mpp.* and kor.mpp.*. For China, Japan and Korea, region data replace country data (18 codes).
A7 country ctf code iso.med.ctf.t uses a different segment order from the world code wld.ctf.med.t, and there are no country/regional ctf rows, so the country branch is dead.
D2 nuclear fuel: L3353 = K2727 (shifted one column: 2022 takes the 2021 value). The value is the typed constant Mitigation!K710:AE710 = 0.004, not Power!G22. No numeric effect.
A15 (tcx) uses A14’s helper $K3110 instead of $K3121 (same value). A15 is labelled “not used in the model at all”.
K5 planned-retirement probe: INDEX(Power!$D$1749:$BD$1878,$I3992,L3990) is offset by one row and three columns from the data range G1750:BD1878; the flag J3991 uses F1750:F1857 while the MATCH uses D1750:D1878. Harmless today.
CoC: countries without fixed data silently get Sri Lanka’s parameters (row 172) as the XLOOKUP if_not_found. Countries absent from CoC rows 202–390 get 0.075 + the tech adjustment.
WACC is time-invariant: only CoC column D (2022) is used, although D:V hold 2022–2040.

title: 6  Road transport
text:
1. What it is
The “technoeconomic” road model of legacy CPAT and of the methodology note (data/source/Transportation_methodology.docx). It projects road vehicles, distance driven, fuel economy and energy use from vehicle economics, instead of the single fuel-use equation of the elasticity approach.

Vehicle classes: passenger and light vehicles (new and used), freight trucks and 2-3 wheelers; buses follow passenger vehicles.
Powertrains: gasoline, diesel, LPG and CNG/LNG; PHEVs (passenger); BEVs.
Fuels covered: road gasoline, diesel, LPG, natural gas and electricity; road biofuels follow them as legacy (v0.4.12, LD62): bioethanol and other biofuels with gasoline, biodiesel with diesel (base year x use / base-year use). The vehicle feebate’s CO2 per liter of gasoline and diesel is scaled by their fossil share in the base year (legacy E2146:E2147; issue I40, replicated). Coal, kerosene and other oil products in road, and rail, aviation and navigation, stay on the elasticity approach.

Switch: ScenarioDefinition TrModel (legacy row 340), per scenario. - Elasticity (default): results are exactly those of v0.3.4. - Engineer: section 5b replaces road gasoline, diesel, LPG, gas and biofuels in section 5 in every year. Road electricity feeds power demand from the year after the base year. CO2, revenues, methane, air pollutants and the totals follow.
Section 5b is computed in every scenario either way, so the two approaches can be compared side by side.


2. How it works (one year at a time)

Vehicle demand:

Passenger ownership per 1,000 people follows a Gompertz curve in GDP per capita. Its saturation level comes from the data, and it adjusts partially each year, with limits on annual growth and decline.
Calibration scales the curve to observed ownership in the last data year, up or down.
Freight and 2-3 wheelers: freight ownership is an income-dependent share of passenger ownership; 2-3 wheelers follow a hump in income.

Stock: vehicles retire at 1/lifetime of the trailing-average stock. Purchases are demand minus the remaining stock, split between new and used vehicles by the used share.
Total cost of ownership (TCO) per km, ICEV and BEV:

Purchase price after customs, ad-valorem tax, VAT, feebates and EV subsidies.
Depreciation and resale value, insurance and maintenance.
Fuel or electricity:

retail prices incl. carbon tax and fuel reform;
EV electricity at last year’s power price plus a charging mark-up that falls with EV penetration.

Distance tax.
Range anxiety for BEVs: it falls as charging stations grow; charging stations grow with the BEV stock and with charging subsidies.
Discounting: at a consumer discount rate that falls with income.

Choice:

EV share of purchases: a logit in TCO per km, separately for new and used passenger vehicles, freight and 2-3 wheelers.
Fuel split among ICEVs: own- and cross-price elasticities of TCO.

Fuel economy:

New vehicles: improves autonomously and with the fuel price (incl. the feebate per liter).
Stock: turns over with purchases.
Distance per vehicle: responds to the cost per km and to income.

Fuel use: vehicles × distance / fuel economy, by class and fuel, in two calibration steps to the base-year energy balance:

distance factors by class;
then a residual factor by fuel.

Buses: base-year bus fuel scales with passenger fuel use by fuel; bus electricity scales with passenger electricity.

Policies: all are scenario rows on ScenarioDefinition (rows 418-479), off by default: - carbon tax, fuel price reform and existing taxes (through the retail prices); - feebates by class (rate per t CO2, pivot); - distance tax; - EV purchase subsidy; - ad-valorem purchase taxes; - VAT and customs on BEVs; - charging-station subsidy.

Size of the bug fixes: the legacy engineer run, with its bugs, gives road fuel a third higher by 2035. The fixes are listed one by one, with their effects, in chapter Transport.

Range anxiety uses legacy’s stored values, solved in another vintage. For Egypt the calculated 2025 passenger EV share is 0.09% against an actual 0.15%. A goal seek for the corrected model is open (the workbook reports the fit).
Calibration factors are large for Egypt: passenger distance × 2.67, then gasoline × 1.23. The Transport1 data explain only part of road fuel use, so review the data.

2. Names, LAMBDAs, constants, data sheets

80 new LAMBDAs (TR_LAMBDAS, notes in TR_LAMBDA_NOTES): ENGINEERON, TRDATA, TRBLEND, OPENING, TRAILAVG, LAGVALUE, RETIRED, MARKUP, STATIONS, RANGEANX, NEWFE, FEEBATE, RATIO, WAVG, MIXTWO, GROWVKT, CLAMPVKT, USEDVKT, DISCKM, COSTKM, DISTTAX, CSRAMP, PIVOTAVG, PIVOTMAN, PIVOTPICK, FBVEH, GROSSUP, POLPICK, EVSUB, ANNUITY, SALVAGE, RESALE, INSMAINT, FUELKM, TOTAL, TOTALRA, TCOFUEL, LOGITICE, ACTSHARE, REST, ACTORCALC, OWNEXP, GOMPTGT, OWNDEM, CLAMPOWN, PLUG, ADDTHREE, TURNOVER, NEWINSTOCK, CROSSRATIO, ICESPLIT, NORMSH, OWNSH, PERTH, OPENFE, STOCKFE, VKTFUEL, TWOFUEL, BEVFENEW, BEVFEOPEN, PHEVELE, EMITFUEL, INTENSITY, INTENS0, KTOE, KTOEELE, BUSFUEL, BUSELE, AVGFE, AVGFEEV, PROD3SUM, BIOSCALE, HOLD, DISCRATE, FRESHARE, CYCHUMP, BEVUPLIFT, INTAVG, ROADSWITCH, DEMROAD. Reused: SCALEBY, DIFF, SHAREOF, ADDED, POSTTAX.
Named constants (sheet Constants): Thousand, Million, Billion, TrRALag (3: range anxiety holds its start value for three years), TrPivotLag (2: feebate pivot blank in the first two years), TrOwnDecline (0.1, fix B4), TrFEWGso, TrFEWHalf, TrFEWEvP, TrFEWEvO (fixed weights of the average fuel economy without fuel use).
Data sheets (DATA group): Transport1 (TrKey, TrVal, TrYr; key country|variable), Transport2 (VPKey, VPVal, VPYr), Transport3 (RAKey, RAPas, RAFre, RACyc, RAPasA, RAPasC, RAFreA, RAFreC, RACycA, RACycC), TransportParams (TrParKey, TrParVal), TransportPaths (TrPathKey, TrPathVal, TrPathYr); TrFuelKey = column B of the result rows 2598-2603 (position of a fuel for the switch).
Mapping: sector labels pas, pau, lgt, fre, cyc, bus; fuel labels phv, bev, ev, ice. Variables: 552 new entries (550 section-5b variables, trsum, enel).



3. ScenarioDefinition rows
Template rows 1-415 unchanged; row 417 heading; rows 418-479 the transport policies (TR_MT: per class passenger / freight / 2-3 wheeler: feebate year, rate, pivot type, manual pivot, pivot decline; distance tax year, start, target year, target; EV subsidy year, amount, change; ad-valorem tax ICEV and BEV baseline and policy, its year; customs year; then VAT years (passenger, 2-3 wheeler), VAT and customs policy factors, charging-subsidy start year and level, target year and level). NameOfParameter Tr<Stem><Pas|Fre|Cyc> (e.g. TrSubAmountPas); defaults are the legacy Dashboard values (data/transport_params.csv), all policies off. Every scenario column gets them; Mitigation finds them through the Mapping table (MT_KEYS) like the other ScenarioDefinition rows. All ScenarioDefinition ranges end at row 479 (MT_END: Mapping, Variables lookups, mt_lookup, mt_setting, the batch emulation; macro constant MT_LAST in CPATScenarios.bas). The Mitigation search range grows to row 8000 (MIT_MAX, macro MIT_MAX_ROW).


4. Switch wiring

Section 5: the elasticity fuel use is now variable enel (the former ener formula, FUELUSE, base year from Inputs). ener = ROADSWITCH($D, tr.sw, result rows 2598:2603, enel); D = Inputs column trpos = position of the fuel in TrFuelKey for road (gasoline 1, diesel 2, LPG 3, gas 4, biofuels 6), 0 elsewhere. With TrModel = Elasticity (default) ener = enel everywhere, so every v0.3.4 output is unchanged (regression 0). With Engineer the road gasoline, diesel, LPG, gas and biofuels of section 5 are those of section 5b in every year (base year: the calibrated value = the energy balance); CO2, revenues, CH4, air pollutants and the totals follow.
Section 3 H: dem = DEMROAD($F, tr.sw, road electricity 2604, previous, multiple); F = Inputs_power column tr (1 for road). From 2023 road electricity demand is the engineer value when switched on (base year: the data).
Biofuels: road biofuels = base year x (gasoline + diesel) / base year of the engineer model (BIOSCALE).
No circular reference: the engineer model reads the power price of the previous year (base year: same year), GDP growth of the previous year and the GDP level after the feedback (which uses last year’s effect); fuel prices do not depend on fuel use.



5. Deviations from the reference and why
The reference engine is reproduced exactly (section 6); the deviations are in the inputs it gets from the prototype:

2-3 wheeler gasoline price: the road gasoline price incl. new policies (as passenger); legacy row 4438 uses the price before new policies, so carbon pricing did not reach 2-3 wheelers.
VAT on vehicles: VAT_WEO of the customs year from Prices_dom (Egypt 0.14; the legacy run had 0.1531).
Industrial gas price for LNG trucks: section 2 industrial price + the road new policies (POSTTAX).
Biofuels: the prototype keeps biofuels as a fuel; the engineer EF adjustment for blending is 1 and road biofuels scale with engineer gasoline and diesel.
Formulas: the charging-subsidy ramp is written as start + (target - start) x MIN(1, (year - start year) / MAX(1, target year - start year)) (same values; no division by zero when the two years are equal); the cross-TCO ratio of the ICE split uses IFERROR for “other fuels without share” (blank, as the reference’s guard); the average EV fuel economy uses a helper row (trafen); the price-response switch of the purchase distance is a 0/1 parameter. All for the 100-character limit; values identical.
Road electricity in the base year of section 3 H stays the data (the engineer value replaces it from 2023).



6. Check results
check_full.py (report check_report_v0.6.4.md):

Section 5b against transport_model_ref.engine(fix=ALL_FIXES), inputs from the Python recomputation (an independent copy of the input mapping, tr_inputs): every row with year values and the side-table parameters (base-year split, purchase taxes, bus fuel), scenarios 1 and 2, as shipped and with the Lambdas library over every row: max relative difference about 4e-14.
Copied scenarios with TrModel = Engineer (11: copy of 1; 12: copy of 2, carbon tax; 13: + EV subsidy; 14: + distance tax; 15: + subsidy, distance tax, feebates, charging subsidy): section 5b vs the engine (max 5e-14) and the whole model vs the Python recomputation with the engine’s road fuels and road electricity (iterated to the fixed point; max 7e-12). Road fuels of section 5 = section 5b; road electricity demand = section 5b from 2023.
Directions (2035 unless noted): carbon tax lowers road fuel use (24,580 -> 22,564 ktoe); EV subsidy raises the passenger EV sales share in 2030 (0.55% -> 3.3%); distance tax lowers passenger distance (285 -> 183 bln km); all policies of 15 lower road fuel use (22,564 -> 14,177 ktoe).
Regression vs v0.3.4: 0 on every shared output code (Elasticity by default); new variables reported as added.
The scenario-copy test (copy of 2 with carbon price 0 = scenario 1) skips the row tr.pol (scenario number > 1), as it skips the scenario number itself.
Python interface changes needed for the check: power_model_ref.engine takes an optional inp['dem_fixed'] (road demand from the engineer model; default behaviour unchanged).

Charging and range anxiety (4334-4356). All bugs and decisions against legacy: chapter Transport.

B14 freight distance. The TCO uses Transport1 average vkt freight (48,630 km, clamped to at least 50,000 km, which binds in every projection year), while fuel use uses 8,091 km (derived from fuel shares) x 1.70. Which freight VKT is right, and should the clamp stay? Not fixed.

B4 value. 10% (legacy 2-3 wheeler value) is a placeholder; no effect for Egypt.
PHEV TCO includes the full BEV range anxiety (about 100,000 $/vehicle), so PHEV sales vanish; keep?
Data years. VAT on vehicles is the 2024 VAT rate, customs the 2024 duties, import shares 2022, bus electricity the 2024 EV stock share (parameters customs_year, import_year, bus_ele_year). Use the last data year instead?
Calibration factors (passenger distance x2.67, then gasoline x1.23): Transport1 ownership x distance / fuel economy explains only 30-60% of Egypt’s road fuel. Report them in the workbook; review the data.
Bus electricity (B6). The fix scales bus electricity with passenger electricity relative to base passenger energy; an explicit bus EV share may be preferable.

Transport1 holds 220 countries (880 rows of 4 years), not 221; Transport3 has stored values for 194 countries.
B4: the 2026 jump (P4787 = 59.25 against O = 55.12) is the 7.5% growth cap binding (55.12 x 1.075), not a closing-stock mismatch.
B2 also hits 2-3 wheelers (4501 = 4487). For freight it has no effect on the TCO distance because the 50,000 km minimum binds; the effect shows only through 2-3 wheelers and BEV freight from 2038.
B6 also mixes units in bus electricity (5318 adds bln liters of diesel, LPG and gas to bln kWh).
B3: with the data to 2025, actual/expected is 55.1/152.1 = 0.36 (the survey’s 57.8/138.9 is the 2024 column used by legacy).
Not in the survey: B19 (new BEV maintenance at the ICEV rate), B20 (used ICEV/BEV depreciation periods differ), B21 (freight VKT output omits LPG/LNG), B22 (gas fuel-economy weights use LPG freight; EV fallback tests diesel); the BEV freight feebate (4637) uses ICEV discounted km (same values); vehicle shares 2078-2081 use the 2022 VKT split in every data year; the Transport3 calibration does not hold in this file (open question 3).

title: 7  Emissions
text:
Non-CO2 GHGs and methane: method
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Emissions.md.
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
The model adds methane, nitrous oxide and F-gases to energy CO2 and covers every UNFCCC inventory category, so it reports total GHG emissions. It includes a methane fee, its revenue, and combustion methane for every sector.
Units: methane in kt CH4 where it is a physical quantity, otherwise Mt CO2e with IPCC AR6 GWP100 (fossil methane 29.8, non-fossil 27.2). GHGYear is the last year the country has in the inventory (Egypt: 2024).

title: 7  Emissions
text:
1. Data








Sheet
Content
Source




GHGs
Inventory by country, year, category (energy, industrial processes, agriculture, LULUCF, waste, other) and gas (CO2, CH4, N2O, F-gases), Mt CO2e
Legacy sheet GHGs


CH4Inputs
Methane abatement curves (a, b) by country and source; shares that split inventory methane by source; flared share
Legacy sheet CH4Inputs


EF_NonCO2
Combustion emission factors (kt per PJ) by country or region, subsector, fuel and pollutant, base year and final
Legacy sheet EF_PM (GAINS; all countries and World Bank regions)


UNPop

Legacy sheet UNPop (UN WPP)


Balances
