Legacy Mitigation rows 503-509



The non-energy elasticities (section 4) are on sheet Manual inputs K325:M327, the legacy addresses (agriculture, waste, other: population elasticity row 326, per capita income elasticity row 327; a text entry such as “na” counts as 0). Their values reproduce the cached results of the legacy run exactly: legacy Mitigation uses the same values (it never reads the manual cells: their formula is broken, #REF!).


2. Methane by source
Seven sources: oil and gas extraction, downstream gas, coal mining and biomass use (fossil methane, part of energy); livestock and rice (agriculture); waste.

Allocation. Inventory methane of each category in GHGYear is split between its sources. Fossil sources: weight = MIN(10 x the source’s share of the four activities, the country’s input share), normalized to sum to 1. Livestock and rice take their input shares; waste takes all waste methane.
Activity. Oil and gas: gas and oil production; coal: coal production (both held at the base-year balance). Downstream gas and biomass: total gas and biomass use of the scenario, power included. Livestock, rice, waste: an index (1 in the base year) that grows with income and population.
Abatement. Fee per tonne CH4 = methane fee (USD per t CO2e) x GWP x 1 if the fee applies to the source (below), else 0. Abatement share = MIN(1, MAX(0, a x fee^b)) on the source’s curve. Biomass and downstream gas use the oil-and-gas curve, as legacy.
Emissions = the source’s inventory methane x activity / activity in GHGYear x (1 - abatement). Shares and GHGYear activity are from scenario 1: the calibration is to the observed (baseline) inventory.
Flaring. The flared share of abated oil and gas methane burns to CO2 (44/16 t CO2 per t CH4), reported as energy CO2.
Revenue = fee x the sum over the sources the fee applies to of CH4 x GWP (fossil or non-fossil), USD million, part of total revenue.
Fiscal space (v0.6.2, I47; user 2026-10-20: as close to legacy as possible with no vulnerability to circular references). The GDP feedback counts the fee revenue as legacy (row 8024) through ch4.revf: the same sum over ch4.emf, which equals ch4.em except for downstream gas and biomass use. Those two read the stored scenario-1 activity (sheet BaselineCO2 rows dg, bm, refreshed by the build; check row ch4bs.chk = 0 in scenario 1), so the fiscal space reads no fuel use and no later change to the demand or power blocks can close a loop through it. Fee, abatement and the other sources are the scenario’s own. The reported revenue (rmf, rtot, block 12e) keeps the own activity. (The v0.6.0 loop came from price-block average ranges that ran into section 11, fixed in v0.6.2.)

The methane fee (ScenarioDefinition) runs linearly from MPLevelStart in MPIntro to MPLevelTarget in MPOutro and keeps its slope after the target year (as legacy). It adds the carbon price when CTforMethane = Yes. As legacy (v0.4.12, user decision 2026-10-18; LD46):

the fee path applies only in policy scenarios (scenario number above 1, legacy row 2238); the carbon price part has no such condition, as legacy row 2239;
a switch per source on sheet Manual inputs J196:J200, the legacy addresses (names MFeeBio, MFeeDG, MFeeFF, MFeeAgr, MFeeWst; shown on Settings rows 47-51): biomass (No), downstream gas, fossil fuel production (oil, gas and coal), agriculture (livestock, rice), waste (all Yes). The switches are legacy inputs outside ScenarioDefinition (NORMS 4: main inputs on ScenarioDefinition, ‘Manual inputs’ the second source).



3. Energy methane and N2O

Combustion methane = fuel use x emission factor, by subsector and fuel, and for power by generation type. The factor is looked up by legacy EF code as for the local pollutants (v0.9.0: country, else World Bank region, else world; table Inputs_nc). Legacy 465 has these lookups but leaves the CH4 factors blank, so its combustion CH4 is zero (issue I34). The factor moves linearly from its base-year value to its final value in 2039 (EFEndYear, the legacy column), flat after.
Energy methane = calibration factor x (combustion + fossil supply methane) x fossil GWP. The factor = inventory energy methane / modelled energy methane in GHGYear (scenario 1). Energy methane thus equals the inventory in GHGYear and later moves with fuel use, supply activity and abatement. v0.6.2: the modelled GHGYear combustion and supply methane of scenario 1 are stored on sheet BaselineCO2 (rows ch4c, ch4sup, refreshed by the build), so the factor, used in every year, reads no later model year (circular-reference rule, user 2026-10-20).
Energy N2O and F-gases: the inventory while it has the year; then N2O moves with energy CO2 and F-gases are held.
Energy CO2 = fuel combustion (power included) + flaring.



4. Other inventory categories
Each category and gas takes the inventory value while the inventory has the year. After that it grows with a growth factor = (1 + GDP per capita growth)^income elasticity x (1 + population growth)^population elasticity x the change in mitigation effort. GDP per capita growth = (1 + real GDP growth) / (1 + population growth) - 1. Effort is 1, or, if ScenarioDefinition AdditionMitigationPoliciesNonEnergy = Yes, the scenario’s energy CO2 divided by scenario 1’s.

5. Validation and differences with legacy

check_full.py recomputes every GHG and combustion-methane row in Python from the data files (scenarios 1 and 2, every year).
When introduced (v0.2.8), every earlier output was unchanged (the methane fee is 0 in the shipped scenarios).
The non-energy elasticities reproduce the legacy run exactly where the legacy method is kept.
Sheet LegacyDiff lists the differences with legacy; the register of bugs, issues and upgrades describes the legacy bugs fixed: L18 (non-energy methane constant, abatement not applied), L19 (flaring CO2 counted as methane), L20 (population growth path), L21 (waste abated with the livestock curve). Local air pollutants: chapter Emissions.



6. Open issues

Egypt’s inventory breaks after 2021 (I91): energy CH4 is 21.9 Mt CO2e in 2021 and 1.9-2.0 in 2022-2024, while the fugitive-emissions memo alone is 20.3 in 2023. Calibrating to 2024 (as legacy) may understate energy methane by about 19 Mt CO2e.
Energy CO2 calibration to the inventory (as legacy since v0.4.11; switch on): every CO2 emission factor is scaled by the 2021 inventory over the 2022 estimate (Egypt 0.930; chapter Emissions); the 2021-2022 inventory break (I91) carries into every year, as legacy.
Combustion factors use only the GAINS base and final values (the yearly paths are proprietary). Combustion methane exceeds inventory energy methane, so the calibration factor is about 0.25 for Egypt.
Oil, gas and coal production is held at the base year (no production model).



Fuel production for supply methane (v0.5.6, I66)
Oil, gas and coal production (rows ch4.prd) start from Balances and hold in the base year and the next, then grow with the producer-price response to the methane fee (ch4.pi = 1 + change of the fee per unit / international price x pass-through, Manual inputs J194; elasticities J190:J192) and the growth of world demand of the global demand scenario a year earlier (ch4.wd, Prices_int rows 323-333), as legacy rows 6132-6149. The methane source shares use base production as the inventory-year activity (no loop).


NDC comparison (v0.5.7, section 14c; legacy F12 rows 18403-18518)
Data: sheet NDCs (legacy NDCs rows 48-242 latest, 250-444 second, 451-644 first round, columns C-P, stacked with a round column; key ISO|round) and sheet GHGHist (legacy GHGs rows 954-1189: GHGs excl./incl. LULUCF, CO2 excl. LULUCF, energy CO2 by year; header group|year). Both from extract_legacy_tables.py ndc.
Choice (ScenarioDefinition scenario 1, as legacy): NDCs (First round, Second round, else the latest), NDCTargetYear (Main* = first target year, else the second where given), Conditionality (Unconditional, Conditional, else the average). Target year at most NDCYrCap (2035).
Target on the NDC’s own basis (gases CO2 or GHGs; LULUCF included or excluded), against the modelled BAU = scenario 1 in the target year: BAU: BAU x (1 + x) (x the reduction as given, negative); Fixed: x (Mt CO2e); Historical: emissions of the reference year (scenario 1 where modelled, from 2022; else the GHGs inventory, 2021-2024, rows ndc.hc and ndc.hv, v0.6.1; else GHGHist) x (1 + x); Intensity: reference-year emissions x real GDP of the target year / real GDP of the reference year x (1 + x); Unquantifiable: BAU. Reduction = 1 - target / BAU, for the unconditional (u) and conditional (c) targets; a = their average (the one given if only one; 0 if none); sel = the Conditionality choice (a if the chosen one is not given). Target GHGs incl. LULUCF = MIN(BAU incl. LULUCF, BAU incl. LULUCF x (1 - reduction)), as legacy rows 18494-18496. Per scenario and year: reduction of GHGs incl. LULUCF against scenario 1 (ndc.red), share of the NDC reduction achieved (ndc.gap = ndc.red / ndc.r.sel, legacy “Gap to NDC”), GHGs above the chosen target (ndc.over; in the target year the legacy goal-seek difference, G18501). No goal seek (user 2026-10-19: comparison only).
Legacy bugs fixed: L119 (year adjustment applied twice for BAU, never for Fixed or Historical: the prototype compares in the target year), L120 (index ratios inverted), L121 (Historical “level” is the cut), L122 (Intensity adds a blank cell for LULUCF), L123 (Intensity reference GDP from a fixed cell). title: 7  Emissions
section: Calibration of energy CO2 to the GHG inventory: method
text:
Calibration of energy CO2 to the GHG inventory: method
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md. Decision and numbers: Old/Calibration_Plan_v3_6.md.

1. Method
Every CO2 emission factor (EF), by subsector and fuel and by generation type, is multiplied by one factor, EFCalib. Since v0.4.11 this is legacy’s rule (user decision 2026-10-18: go with legacy; issue I32 replicated): legacy Mitigation rows 623, 839 and 976-977.
EFCalib = inventory energy CO2 of the year before the base year / scenario-1 energy CO2 of the base year with uncalibrated EFs (the base-year energy balance x the EFs); 1 if the switch is off. The switch is Settings C27, Yes by default, as legacy (EFsAdjustmentAnnexI and EFsAdjustmentNonAnnexI are both Yes*). With the shipped data (Egypt): 2021 inventory 211.05 Mt against the 2022 estimate 226.97 Mt, EFCalib = 0.930 (legacy: 0.930).
The uncalibrated scenario-1 CO2 is data written by the build, like the ETS baseline: a live formula would be circular (EFs feed carbon prices, which feed fuel use). Scenario-1 fuel use does not depend on the EFs in value (no new carbon price; existing carbon pricing changes only after the historical years), so the calibrated baseline is the uncalibrated one times the factor. The rows are keyed by country (EGY|raw, EGY|pow, …), so another country finds no rows (#N/A) rather than Egypt’s: rebuild with its code (about 2 minutes since v0.4.9), or paste its scenario-1 values under its key.
Everything downstream follows: CO2 by subsector, fuel and power type; carbon tax, ETS cost and existing carbon pricing per unit of fuel and their revenue; the ETS baseline; energy CO2 in the GHG totals. title: 7  Emissions
text:
Local air pollutants: method
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
The model computes emissions of seven local air pollutants from the fuel use of every subsector and of power generation: fine particulate matter (PM2.5), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulphur dioxide (SO2), volatile organic compounds (VOC), black carbon (BC), organic carbon (OC) and carbon monoxide (CO). A memo converts them into CO2 equivalents (forcing). The emissions are also grouped into the sectors of the legacy air-pollution module, with primary organic matter and other PM2.5, its inputs. The pollutants are not part of the GHG totals. LiveOutputs reports total PM2.5, NOx, SO2, black carbon and the forcing for every scenario; the Charts sheet plots PM2.5 and SO2.
Units: emissions in kt; factors in t per ktoe; forcing in Mt CO2e (GWP100).

1. Data

The factors are those of legacy 465 (Mitigation rows 1052-1663; v0.9.0), in a table by legacy EF code on sheet Inputs_nc (Inputs, merged view):

the legacy EF subsector of each subsector: road, rail, aviation (jet fuel), residential, services, construction, other manufacturing, food & forestry and other energy keep their own code; mining & chemicals, iron & steel, other metals, machinery, cement and fuel transformation take manufacturing (mnf, legacy rows 6388-6395); navigation, which legacy leaves out (bug L22), takes its own GAINS code nav;
the factor of the country (egy.mit.ef.<sub>.<fuel>.<pollutant>), else of its World Bank region (CtryReg, Egypt mea), else of the world (wld, absent from the data), else 0;
other energy (oen) takes, for each fuel and pollutant, the maximum factor across the other legacy subsectors (power included), as the legacy note says (issue I147);
only the fuel and subsector pairs of the legacy table have factors (power: coal, gas, oil, biomass; road: gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, gas; rail: diesel; aviation: jet fuel; residential: no gasoline or diesel); a pair or pollutant with no factor in the chain gives 0, as legacy (for example power biomass, road kerosene, residential oil, construction coal, gas, oil and biomass, services and other manufacturing coal; organic carbon and SO2 of LPG). None of these pairs burns fuel in Egypt.

The country-region-world chain covers the cases that bugs L58 (subsectors without a GAINS match) and L59 (fuels without a GAINS factor) fixed in v0.2.9 and v0.4.12 (nearest GAINS match): the CPAT team fixed them in 465. Egypt 2022: food & forestry diesel, residential and fuel-transformation LPG, other-manufacturing diesel and LPG take the Middle East & North Africa factors, as legacy.


2. Method

Factor path: the weight of the final factor rises linearly from 0 in the base year to 1 in 2039 (EFEndYear) and stays at 1, as for combustion CH4.
Emissions: for each subsector and pollutant, the sum over the eight fuels of fuel use x the weighted factor. Fuel use is the modelled one, so prices, policies and scenarios carry through. Power uses the same equation over the nine generation types.
Totals: transport, buildings and industry sum their subsectors, navigation included. A pollutant’s total is the subsectors plus power.
Forcing (memo): emissions x the region’s GWP100 for BC, OC, NOx, SO2, VOC and CO, and their sum. Cooling pollutants (OC, SO2, NOx) have a negative GWP, so the net forcing can be negative: about -17.5 Mt CO2e for Egypt in 2022.
Air-pollution module sectors: coal power plants and gas power plants (fuel use of the type x the power factors); other power plants (power less coal and gas); ground level road (road); ground level other (residential, services, construction); other (rail, aviation, navigation, industry without construction, other energy use); food & forestry. The seven sectors add up to the pollutant’s total.
Primary organic matter (POM) and other PM2.5, per sector: POM = 1.3 x organic carbon; other PM2.5 = MAX(0, PM2.5 - black carbon - POM).
The module’s input table (v0.3.12): the block takes the layout of the legacy input table (Mitigation rows 15859-15961):

one block per module sector (coal, gas and other power plants, ground level road, ground level other, other, food & forestry) and one for all sectors;
in each block the ten pollutants in legacy order: NOx, SO2, BC, POM, other PM2.5, VOC, CH4, CO, PM2.5, OC;
codes aps.<pollutant>.<sector>, in kt (legacy: tonnes).

The air-pollution module reads these rows directly (NORMS 3c).
CH4 in the table, as legacy (issue I34):

coal, gas and other power plants: combustion CH4 of the generation types (section 14);
road, ground level other: combustion CH4 of their subsectors (ch4 rows of sections 5-8);
other: combustion CH4 of its subsectors plus fossil fuel supply methane (ch4.sup; legacy has oil and gas extraction only);
food & forestry: combustion CH4 plus agriculture (livestock, rice) and waste methane, as legacy.

Legacy has no combustion CH4 factors, so its combustion part is zero. CH4 here is uncalibrated: it is not scaled to the inventory (ghg.k).

v0.9.0 (factors of legacy 465): in 2022 every module sector equals the legacy input table (rows 15844-16053, tonnes) for every pollutant except “other”, which adds navigation (bug L22: NOx +14.8 kt, SO2 +13.7 kt, BC +0.6 kt, PM2.5 +1.5 kt), and CH4 (combustion CH4 and all fuel supply methane, issue I34). In 2030 the sectors differ from legacy by the fuel-use paths (gas plants 0.88, other plants 0.62, road 0.70-0.77, food & forestry 0.58 of legacy), not by the factors.
The check recomputes all rows of the block in Python for scenarios 1 and 2.


4. Differences with legacy CPAT (sheet LegacyDiff)

Legacy omits navigation from the pollutant totals (bug L22). It is included here.
Legacy leaves services and food & forestry out of each pollutant’s total (bug L23), although its air-pollution sectors include them. Here the total is the sum of the sectors.
Bugs L58 and L59 (subsectors and fuels without a GAINS factor) were fixed by the CPAT team in 465 (country, else region, else world factors); the prototype follows 465 (v0.9.0) and keeps 0 where the 465 chain has no factor, as no such pair burns fuel in Egypt.
Other energy takes the maximum factor of the fuel across the other subsectors (issue I147). Legacy takes the maximum year by year; the prototype the maximum of the base and of the final factors with the line between them, the same where one subsector holds the maximum throughout (Egypt: other oil products, the only fuel of other energy).
Food & forestry is split into food and forestry/agriculture as legacy (v0.4.11, LD53): the food share of each fuel is info_food over the four info_ flows of the processed Balances (legacy rows 501-504, 1666-1673); rows apfd (food fuel use) and ap..fod / .fag (memo rows, not in the totals). The share is 0 for Egypt.
Legacy has no ammonia (NH3) from fuel combustion, so neither does the prototype.
Legacy reads factor paths by year, which are proprietary and empty in the NoPropData file. The prototype draws a linear path between the base and final factors (simplification, as for CH4).

title: 8  Emissions trading (new ETS)
text:
1. Inputs







Input
Notes

Constant keeps the cap level after the target year; any other value keeps the relative change

Sector coverage (ScenarioDefinition)
17 ETS sectors: power plus the 16 subsectors


Benchmarks by sector group (power, transport, residential/buildings, industry)
Share of a sector’s emission intensity allocated free = 1 - the auctioned proportion of ScenarioDefinition rows 90-91 (start, target year) of the scenario, the same for every group, as legacy (v0.4.15, issue I21). Default 1.0: nothing auctioned, the legacy default. After the target year the target share is held (legacy drops it to 0 unless the continuation is Constant: bug L78). Benchmarks by sector come later.


Semi-elasticities by ETS sector
Legacy ETS+LTS table by country and sector group (power, transport, residential, industry; food and services use industry), sheet ETSSemi, looked up by the country code (v0.3.3; legacy Mitigation rows 1815-1831); used only by the fast estimate

Scenario-1 CO2 by ETS sector, stored as data and refreshed by the build (with a check)


Effectiveness of output-based allocation; convergence exponent
0.5 and 0.5 (legacy hardcodes)





2. Price

A covered sector counts once the ETS applies.
Benchmarks run linearly from the start to the target year, flat afterwards. The output-based rebating (OBR) share of a sector = its group’s benchmark, bounded to 0-1.
Volatility adjustment = (1 + carbon tax policy risk x impact) / (1 + ETS volatility x impact). At Medium: (1 + 0.2 x 0.5) / (1 + 0.42 x 0.5) = 1/1.1.
Cap = baseline covered emissions x (1 + change), with the change linear from the start to the target year (after it, per the continuation input).
Effective semi-elasticity = baseline-weighted average over covered sectors of semi-elasticity x (1 − (1 − OBR effectiveness) x OBR share); OBR effectiveness is a setting (Settings C14, legacy value 0.5).
Fast estimate = LN(cap / baseline covered) / (effective semi-elasticity x volatility adjustment) when the cap is below the baseline; else 0.
Permit price = the override prices if the override switch is Yes (a blank year takes the carbon price path), else the fast estimate; 0 before the ETS applies.
Tax-equivalent price = permit price x volatility adjustment; revenue factor = 1 / volatility adjustment.



3. Effect on fuel use and revenue
The ETS replaces the carbon tax in covered sectors. The tax-equivalent price splits by the OBR share:

Price wedge (auctioned part) = tax-equivalent price x EF x coverage x (1 − OBR share). It enters the after-tax fuel price, so usage and efficiency both respond, as for a carbon tax.
Shadow price (OBR part) = tax-equivalent price x EF x coverage x OBR share, added to the feebate shadow price. It acts only on the efficiency margin of fuel use, as feebates do.

New-policy revenue includes the price wedge x the revenue factor: the permit price on the auctioned part of covered emissions. The OBR part raises no revenue.


4. Meeting the cap
The fast estimate uses one semi-elasticity, so the full model does not hit the cap exactly. The model reports CO2 by ETS sector, covered emissions, the cap, the gap (covered / cap − 1) and a proposed price p x (LN(cap/baseline) / LN(covered/baseline)) ^ 0.5. To meet the cap, either:

paste the proposed prices into the override row (with the override switch on) and repeat; or
run the goal seek: the macro SolveETSLive (live scenario; RunAllScenarios runs it for every definition with a new ETS and no override), or python ets_goalseek.py WORKBOOK.xlsx <scenario>, which writes the prices to ets_override_s<scenario>.csv for pasting into the override row. Both iterate with legacy’s damped log-space step (mixing, smoothing, adaptive step) and stop when the worst yearly gap |covered / cap − 1| is below the maximum error, or after the maximum number of iterations.

The goal-seek settings are on sheet Manual inputs at their legacy addresses, as legacy (one value for all scenarios):

The values are those the goal seek has always used here; the legacy defaults are given for reference (the legacy error is measured on its own convergence criterion). A cell that is not a positive number falls back to 20 iterations and 0.005.


5. Limits

Power is covered like any other sector: the power model gives its emissions, and the ETS cost enters its generation cost.
Benchmarks are relative to current emission intensity, and output is proxied by fuel use. Free allocation therefore moves with emissions, and the OBR share equals the benchmark.
The volatility adjustment scales behaviour (the tax-equivalent price), not the permit price. VAT on new policies is levied on the tax-equivalent ETS cost.
No banking, borrowing, price floors or ceilings, and no CBAM process emissions.

text:
Legacy ETS algorithm and a benchmark-based design for the prototype
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
Background note on the legacy algorithm and the design choice behind the prototype’s ETS; the prototype method is in chapter ETS.
Source: CPAT 1.0pre_456_NoPropData.xlsb, sheet Mitigation rows 1797–1969 and 2244–2425, sheet Manual inputs O15:AB15, and VBA Module1 (OverrideETSFast, SolveFast). Row numbers are legacy rows. Formulas not stored in the dump are inferred from the row labels and cached values and marked (inferred).

1. Legacy inputs







Rows
Item




1800–1809

Risk premium inputs: price volatility 0.42, impact 0.5, policy risk 0.2

Sector table: included flag, baseline emissions, semi-elasticity of emissions to the carbon price (power −0.00279, transport −0.00283, residential −0.00386, industry −0.00549, CBAM −0.001 per $/t), generic proportions


1843
Relative price of auctioned ETS vs tax for the same emissions target: 1.1

Relative effectiveness, hardcoded: auctioning 1.0, output-based allocation (OBA/OBR) 0.5



Allocation is one time path of the auctioned share a (rows 1863–1864; OBA share 1 − a), the same for every covered sector.


2. Legacy fast estimate (no iteration)

Covered semi-elasticity (row 1845): coverage-weighted average of the sector semi-elasticities, ε = −0.00288 in the cached run. The all-sector average used for the carbon tax (row 1844) is −0.00371.
Reduction left for the ETS (rows 1858–1860): the reduction needed by the cap minus that of other policies, counted as an effective carbon price × ε_tax (row 1859, e.g. $50/t × −0.00371 = −18.6%).
Effectiveness of the allocation mix (row 1866): e = a × 1.0 + (1 − a) × 0.5.
Adjusted semi-elasticity (row 1867): ε_adj = ε × e. With full OBA, −0.00288 × 0.5 = −0.00144, matching the cached value.
Estimated price (row 1868, QuickEstimateOfETSPrices): p ≈ (reduction left for the ETS) / ε_adj (inferred: linear semi-elasticity form).

This closed-form estimate ignores the full fuel-demand model, where the response comes from prices × elasticities by fuel and subsector, not from one semi-elasticity.


3. Legacy override and goal seek (VBA)

Row 1872 reads override prices from Manual inputs O15:AB15 (OverrideOfETSPrices); row 1873 uses them when the override switch is on.
The full model computes covered emissions with the ETS (rows 1888–1953) and compares the actual reduction with the cap (rows 1956–1963: actual, cap, difference, ratio, error per year; max error in J1963).
The workbook proposes a corrected price per year (PricesAdjustedByErrorFactor): p × (target log-reduction / actual log-reduction)^0.5 (convergence factor 0.5, row 1966).
OverrideETSFast switches the ETS and the override on and calls SolveFast, a damped fixed-point iteration in log space:

If StartFresh, seed the override row from the quick estimate.
Step p ← p × (r/p)^α, with r the workbook’s proposal.
Anderson-style mixing: 0.7 new + 0.3 previous iterate.
Smoothing: 5% weight on a centred 3-year moving average.
Negative or invalid values keep the old price.
Write back, recalculate, take the worst-year error over all 14 years. (The named WorstYearlyETSError averages only 9 years, so the macro bypasses it.)
Halve α if the error got worse (minimum 0.0625); multiply it by 1.2 if the error more than halved (maximum 1).
Stop when the worst error < ETSErrorTolerance or after ETSMaxIterations.

The cached run has override prices of about $22–28/t for 2028–2038, with jumps (1.5 in 2027, 13.8 in 2040) and a max error of 0.33. It had not converged; the cap rows are 0 in the cached state.



4. Legacy split of the price (the same in both parts)








Part
Legacy rows
What it does




Auctioned
1875–1879, 2252 (egy.mit.etstraj)
p × a enters fuel prices as a price wedge, like a carbon tax: fuel switching, efficiency and usage all respond. It raises revenue.


OBA / OBR
1881–1885, 2343–2349 (“Feebate plus non-auctioned ETS”), 2402–2419
p × (1 − a) enters as a shadow price on the efficiency margin only, like a feebate: no pass-through to consumer prices, no revenue.



The legacy note on rows 1875–1885 says “Arguably this should be an exp/ln function TBC”: the split is linear in p. This is also why OBA effectiveness is 0.5: only the efficiency share of the response is triggered, about half of the total with the default elasticities.


5. prototype design: benchmarks instead of one auction share
The legacy auctioned proportion is replaced by benchmarks per covered subsector. Everything after the split stays as in section 4.

Inputs per subsector: the covered flag and a benchmark path b(t), a share of the subsector’s base-year emission intensity (e.g. 0.9 → free allocation at 90% of base-year intensity; a declining path tightens it).
Shares: free allocation FA = b × base-year intensity × output, with output proxied by baseline fuel use (the prototype has no output variable). OBR share s = MIN(FA / covered emissions, 1); auctioned share a = 1 − s. To first order s ≈ b (intensity unchanged). Using actual covered emissions would be circular through fuel use, so the recommendation is scenario-1 (baseline) covered emissions, as in option A of ETS_Cap_Design_Options_v6_4.md; s is then a data-driven input.
Then as legacy: effectiveness e = a + 0.5 × s per subsector; the auctioned part p × a is a price wedge (revenue = p × (covered emissions − FA)); the OBR part p × s joins the sector shadow price (the feebate channel); the fast estimate p = (reduction left for the ETS) / (ε × e), with ε and e weighted by covered baseline emissions.
Override: an offline goal seek (a Python script with the same damped log-space step) writes a row of prices to paste. No VBA and no circular reference.

Without benchmarks the ETS is fully effective (permit price = carbon price path × coverage, as effective as a carbon tax, per an earlier user decision), and the auction share only affects revenue. With benchmarks, the OBR part moves from the price wedge to the shadow price, so emissions fall less for the same p and revenue falls. A benchmark of 0 (full auctioning) reproduces the fully effective case exactly.


6. Open points

The fast estimate uses legacy’s sector semi-elasticities. The prototype could derive them from its own elasticities (one-off calibration run) to keep them consistent.
Legacy’s linear split (p × a) vs a log form (legacy’s own TBC note).
Legacy’s relative price 1.1 (auctioned ETS vs tax) and the risk-premium inputs (rows 1811–1813) are not used by the fast estimate as cached. Check their role before carrying them over.
The CBAM sector semi-elasticity (−0.001) is not modelled in the prototype.

GDP effects: method
Source: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/methods/Macro_and_results.md.

The model estimates how spending the revenue gained by the policies changes GDP. The change feeds back into GDP growth, which drives fuel use, power demand and the non-energy GHG drivers. The method follows legacy CPAT section 17, with legacy bug L24 fixed.

title: 9  Macro, revenues and results
text:
1. Inputs (Egypt defaults)

Revenue use, % of revenue (ScenarioDefinition): labour tax cuts 30, corporate tax cuts 0, public investment 50, current spending 0, targeted transfers 20.
Multiplier source (ScenarioDefinition row 226): Global, income group, Estimated or Manual; Egypt: income group (LMIC). Range Base/Low/High (row 263): Base. Start year for GDP calculations (row 236, GDPStartYear): 2025. Endogenous GDP effects: Yes.
Fiscal multipliers by group, instrument and lag 0-19 (sheet Multipliers, from the legacy sheet: MFMod medians). Low and high are the median minus and plus one standard deviation. Lags 12-19 hold the lag-11 value, as in legacy. v0.4.15 (LD56): “Estimated” takes the country’s table of the legacy Multipliers tab (rows 210-1620, exact match of the country code; the income group where the country is missing, and for CIT and WAGE, whose legacy tables are empty or wrong: bug L76); “Manual” takes sheet Manual inputs J261:U268 (legacy addresses, lags 0-11, blank = 0). Low and high add -/+ the income group’s standard deviation to these too, as legacy (issue I44). Any other source text means the income group.
Baseline real GDP (sheet WEO): 547 USD bn in 2022.



2. Method

Fiscal space (v0.4.15, LD55): total revenue of the scenario (existing taxes net of subsidies plus new policies, power included: rnet + rnew, v0.4.16 + subsidy reform rsr and producer subsidies rpsu, as legacy’s rev.new.usd = row 8026, the total of all instruments) minus that of scenario 1, as a share of GDP. Lower fuel use also lowers the cost of existing subsidies (base erosion), and that counts. Scenario 1 has no GDP effect.
Impulse (v0.4.15, as legacy row 14356): the change of that revenue gain in USD over this year’s GDP, 0 before GDPStartYear (issues I41, I42). Each impulse starts a cohort that acts for 20 years (lags 0-19), lag 0 in the impulse year (legacy applies lag 1 there: bug L68).
Effect of each use: its share x the sum of impulse x multiplier over the lags. The revenue itself counts as an energy-tax increase (instrument exc, share -1). The uses map to labour tax (pit), corporate tax (cit), public investment (capt), current spending (gnfs) and transfers (trns).
GDP effect: the sum over uses (0 if endogenous effects are off): the change of the GDP level against the baseline, as a share of GDP.
Feedback: the GDP level is 1 + last year’s GDP effect, and growth follows from the baseline growth and the change in that level. The one-year lag avoids a circular reference (revenue depends on fuel use, which depends on growth). Legacy instead adds the effect to the growth rate every year, so a steady effect compounds (L24).



2b. Timing rule (stated v0.6.2, issue I72; user 2026-10-20)
Revenue of year t changes GDP only from year t+1. gdp.lvl(t+1) = 1 + gdp.eff(t), and GDP growth after the feedback reads that level (as legacy row 8776, which reads the previous column). Three consequences, kept as rules:

The fiscal space of year t reads revenue of year t only (no later year, no whole-row lookup).
A same-year GDP effect never reaches same-year demand: the impulse of year t counts at lag 0 in gdp.eff(t), which acts on GDP from t+1.
Every other block must not read a later year (NORMS, circular references). With this lag, no revenue line can then close a circular reference, whatever it reads (fuel use, power, methane).

The quick check tests the reads of later years; a change that breaks the lag must restate this rule and pass the full recalculation (Err:522).

Fiscal space jumps to about 0.75% of GDP when the policies start (v0.4.15: total revenue; v0.4.14, new-policy revenue only: 0.55% in 2030). The revenue first lowers GDP: the excise multiplier peaks two years after the impulse. From the early 2030s public investment and transfers outweigh it, and GDP ends about 0.4% above the baseline. The effect raises fuel use a little through the income elasticities.


4. Choices and differences with legacy (sheet LegacyDiff)

L24 fixed: the effect raises the GDP level, not the growth rate every year.
Revenue (v0.4.15): total revenue, as legacy (the v0.3.1 reading “new-policy revenue only” misread legacy’s code rev.new.usd, which is the total). v0.6.2: the methane fee revenue is included as legacy, on the stored scenario-1 activity of downstream gas and biomass use (ch4.revf, issue I47: no vulnerability to circular references; none for Egypt). v0.4.16: fis.rev adds its parts (rnet + rnew + rsr + rpsu); the v0.4.15 form rtot - rmf still referenced the methane fee and LibreOffice reported a circular reference (Err:522) on a full recalculation (found by the paste test’s batch emulation).
Impulse and start year (v0.4.15): as legacy (I41, I42). Not replicated: legacy sets the revenue-use shares to 0 before CPIntro, so earlier impulses count only as an excise drag (I43, tiny for Egypt).
Legacy bugs fixed: L68 (lag 1 in the impulse year), L69 (first cohort’s excise drag lost), L76 (Estimated multipliers).
Scenario-1 lookups stop at the current year, which avoids a circular reference with the GDP feedback. Values are unchanged.
Legacy benchmark: the NoPropData file strips the baseline GDP-effect rows to 0, but the policy rows 14584-14607 hold the cached values of its carbon-tax run (GDP effect 2030 -0.07%, 2035 +0.34%, 2040 +1.22%; its carbon price rises to about 175 $/t in 2041, so it is not the prototype scenario). The check compares the workbook with an independent Python recomputation that iterates the whole model on the growth path until it converges (growth depends only on earlier years).



5. Memo rows (v0.5.7; legacy F4 rows 16163-16201)

Legacy rows 16166-16175 add the effects to growth every year (L24), so its channel values are not comparable.

2. 12d Fiscal reports (v0.3.13; legacy section 16 info rows, F9)
Revenue by fuel, net of subsidies (USD m real). Each fuel covers existing taxes, subsidies and new-policy revenue: - rfu.<fuel>: rtx + rsub + rnew of the fuel over all subsectors. The formula is SUMPRODUCT(SUMIFS(..., SecVar, {"rtx","rsub","rnew"}, SecFuel, fuel)). - rfu.ecy: electricity, i.e. VAT, the subsidy gap and VAT on the policy cost passed through (rvat + rgap + rnvat, section 3 G). - rfg.<type>: fuels burnt in power generation (coal, gas, oil, biomass): prtx + prxc + prsub + prnew of the type (section 3 M; Q28). - rfu.chk: ABS(sum of the rows - rnet.all - rnew.all). It is 0, because the rows split the section 12 totals exactly. The methane fee (rmf) is not a fuel revenue.
12e. Total revenue by policy (v0.4.15, LD37; legacy rows 8016-8027, USD m real). The legacy split of total revenue by instrument: - rpol.ct new carbon tax = SUMPRODUCT(covct, ctr) over the coverage sectors (covered CO2 x the sector’s carbon tax rate; power included); rpol.ets auctioned ETS = SUMPRODUCT(co2.sec, etr) x ets.rf; of which power: rpol.ctp, rpol.etp. - rpol.exc new excise (fuel price reform) = the per-pair rows rex (fuel use x PJ/ktoe x ntx) + power prnew - ctp - etp. - rpol.vat VAT = the per-pair rows rvt (fuel use x PJ/ktoe x (vat + (xcpd + nce) x VAT rate)) + electricity VAT (rvat, rnvat). - rpol.psu producer subsidies = the electricity subsidy gap (rgap, legacy E for electricity; oil, coal and gas producer subsidies follow with LD19). - rpol.exi existing taxes and subsidies = rnet + rnew - the rows above (fuel use x (excise + change in existing carbon pricing) + consumer subsidies + power fuel taxes and subsidies). - rpol.ren renewable subsidies and rpol.trs transport revenues: 0 (not modelled; issue I46); rpol.mf methane fee = rmf; rpol.tot = their sum = rtot (check row rpol.chk). Egypt, carbon tax scenario, 2030: carbon tax 4.2 bn USD (power 1.8), existing taxes and subsidies -10.3 bn, electricity subsidy gap -10.0 bn, total -16.1 bn. Legacy bugs L70-L73 and L75 do not arise (each pair takes its own rates, uses and coverage).
Revenue against GDP and base erosion. - rbe: base erosion, i.e. rnet - rnet of scenario 1 in the same year. This is the change in existing taxes net of subsidies when a policy changes fuel use (Q25: policy fuel use x baseline tax rates, against baseline revenue). Egypt, carbon tax scenario, 2030: about +1.5 bn USD. Fuel use falls, so subsidies (negative) shrink more than existing taxes. - rpct.<x>: shares of baseline real GDP, via GDPSHARE in the LAMBDA column. They cover: - total revenue; - existing taxes net of subsidies; - subsidies; - new-policy revenue; - change in total revenue against scenario 1; - base erosion.
Egypt 2022: total revenue -8.6% of GDP, because consumer subsidies exceed taxes.
LiveOutputs rows: rpct.all.tot, .chg, .sub, .be; rbe.all.all.
Not built (TODO; decisions taken during the run, to confirm): - Producer subsidies (Q26). There are no data for Egypt, and NORMS 3c bars zero placeholders. - Revenue lost to price controls (Q29). Legacy holds only pass-through coefficients (rows 746-760, 2216-2220), not a revenue row. - Fuel expenditures. These are the spending rows of the section 2 memo (pav.sp, v0.3.10), so they are not repeated here. - Vehicle revenues of the road engineer model in 12b (Q27). Planned for later.


3. 11b Energy consumption: change against scenario 1 (v0.3.14; legacy F7)
echg rows give the change against scenario 1 in the same year, in ktoe. The levels come from section 11: - by fuel, from the fuel rows (power generation fuels included); - by sector group, from the sector totals of sections 5-8; - power generation fuel use; - the total.
The change is read through helper row 10 (INDEX(scenario 1 .. this column, position of scenario 1's year)).
epct rows give the % change: echg / (level - echg), and 0 when scenario 1 is 0.
Not as rows: the energy-balance matrix (legacy G; Q30). It is a rearrangement of section 11 and goes to an output sheet later.


4. 13b CO2 change, grid emission intensity, Kaya identity (v0.3.14; legacy F13, row 6582, F14)
CO2 change. cchg gives the change of CO2 from fuel combustion against scenario 1, by fuel and by sector group, power included (MtCO2).
Grid intensity. co2.grid = CO2 of power generation x Million / (total generation in MWy x HoursYr), in tCO2 per MWh. Egypt: 0.41 in 2022 (legacy 0.38) and 0.33 in 2030.
Kaya identity (legacy rows 18877-18893), as legacy (v0.3.18): - GDP: baseline real GDP (the header row), in every scenario. - CO2: total CO2 including industrial processes (ghg.g.co2). - Energy: total primary energy supply, kaya.tpes (legacy row 18880). It is the fuel use of section 11 (fuels burnt in power plants included, biomass included), plus primary electricity: the energy input pe of nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables in section 3. The input is generation divided by the type’s efficiency (physical energy content method: nuclear at 38%, renewables at about 1). Egypt 2022: 89,471 ktoe = legacy 89,471. Energy intensity 163.57 ktoe per USD bn = legacy.
v0.3.14-v0.3.17 used fuel use only (2.6% lower in 2022). This was corrected at the user’s request (2026-10-16). Legacy’s broken “simplified Kaya” row (18931, -97%) is a different row and is not used.

Later: the NDC comparison (Q33; needs the NDC table).


6. Section 17 Carbon pricing (v0.3.15; legacy F3, F5d-e)
Implicit carbon price by fuel (cpi.<fuel>, USD per tCO2). Revenue net of subsidies of the fuel, divided by its CO2: - revenue: existing taxes + subsidies + new policies, final use (rfu) and power generation (rfg); - CO2: from section 13.
This is legacy’s “total carbon price” by fuel (F5d), which divides the tax-and-subsidy wedge per GJ by the emission factor. cpi.all is the same over the fossil fuels.
Biomass is left out (Q34): it has no CO2, and legacy gives #DIV/0!. Egypt 2022: gas -151, diesel -249, LPG -280, all fossil fuels -179 USD per tCO2 (subsidies). A carbon tax of 20 USD raises every fuel by about 20.
Effective carbon rate (ecr, legacy row 16662). (rnet + rnew) / energy CO2, as legacy, so VAT, the electricity subsidy gap and electricity VAT count (issue I36: the OECD rate counts carbon taxes, excises and permit prices only). Egypt 2022: -207 USD per tCO2 (legacy -122; the price data differ).
Effective carbon tax (cpeff, legacy row 16137). Carbon price x the share of energy CO2 it covers.
Coverage. - covct.<sector>: CO2 covered by the new carbon tax in each of the 17 coverage sectors. It is the CO2 of the fuels whose switch is on (fc rows), counted only where the sector’s carbon-tax rate is above 0. A sector in a non-complementary ETS has none. Power uses the CO2 of coal, gas and oil generation. - cov.ct.<group>, cov.ct.all: shares of national energy CO2 (legacy rows 16152-16157). Egypt, carbon tax scenario, 2030: 99.8% (legacy 98.8%), of which power 41%. - cov.ets: ETS coverage share (from co2.ets). - cov.all: their sum.
The cpi, ecr, cpeff and coverage-share rows call SAFEDIV / SCALEBY in the LAMBDA column.

title: 9  Macro, revenues and results
section: Multiple scenarios: definitions, batch run, stored results, comparison
text:
Multiple scenarios: definitions, batch run, stored results, comparison
Equations: Equations.md; workbook formulas: Formulas.md.
The model calculates two scenarios at a time: the baseline and one live policy scenario. A batch macro copies each scenario definition into the live scenario, calculates it and stores its results as values, which are compared afterwards. This follows legacy CPAT, where a macro copies each scenario column into the column used for calculation and stores the outputs.

1. Where things are







Place
What it holds




ScenarioDefinition, scenario 1
The baseline, stored once.


ScenarioDefinition, scenario 2
The live policy scenario. The batch run overwrites it with each definition and restores it at the end.


ScenarioDefinition, columns to the right
Scenario definitions, one full ScenarioDefinition column each: short name (row 2, the legend in the charts), Run? (Yes/No), number (previous + 1), name, then the inputs. Red cells differ from the template. To add one, copy the last definition one column to the right and edit it. Blank columns are grouped and collapsed.


Mitigation, Distribution
Two scenario groups: 1 = the baseline (plain formulas), 2 = the live scenario (every calculated cell calls its named LAMBDA). More live scenarios: copy group 2 to the right and set its scenario number; LiveOutputs has room for 12 scenario blocks.


LiveOutputs
The key indicators of every scenario group, one block per scenario, found on Mitigation by output code.


StoredOutputs
Results as values only: the LiveOutputs indicators of each scenario, under its ID and output code (country.stem.ID). ID 1 is the baseline; a definition keeps its ScenarioDefinition number. Sorted by indicator, then ID (like variables together); every lookup matches the output code, so any order works.


ScenarioCompare
The dashboard and every user entry of the front: results from Live (LiveOutputs) or Stored (StoredOutputs), the year, the data source of the linked tables. Core buttons (green) and the others (grey); key results for one year of up to 10 scenarios against the baseline; a bar chart; time series with their chart beside them.


VBA module CPATScenarios
The macros below. The workbook is an .xlsm; the source is also in CPATScenarios.bas.


MacroCheck
Report of the first-run test macro CheckBatchRun.





2. Shipped definitions

4

Paths continue after their target year as set in the model: the carbon price follows its ScenarioDefinition switch, and feebates continue linearly.


2b. Main scenario choice and regulations as shadow prices (v0.4.16, LD9)
ScenarioDefinition row 13 (ScenarioSelected, ” - Carbon tax” in every shipped scenario) picks a row of the legacy scenario table (legacy Mitigation rows 222-262, columns N:AC; sheet Mapping, block “Main scenarios”): whether the scenario prices carbon explicitly (legacy row 259), its efficiency adjustment (ScenarioDefinition rows 247-251) and the sectors its shadow price covers (rows 240-257).

Explicit scenarios (carbon tax, total carbon price, coal excise, road fuel tax, electricity emissions tax and excise): the carbon price path of ScenarioDefinition rows 18-21 is the carbon tax (cpx = cptraj), as before.
Shadow-pricing scenarios (feebates, power supply feebates, energy efficiency regulations, power feebate, vehicle fuel economy, residential and industrial efficiency regulations; and “Baseline”): no explicit carbon tax (cpx = 0); the carbon price path becomes a shadow price on the efficiency margin, reg.<sector> = cp.shd x the scenario’s adjustment (energy efficiency 247, vehicle fuel economy 248, residential 249, industrial 250, feebates 251; Egypt 0.7, feebates 1) x 1 if the scenario covers the sector. It enters shpx (with the feebate part, now x row 251, and the ETS benchmark part), so fuel use responds through efficiency only, and power through shk (legacy bugs L87, L88 fixed: legacy’s regulation share is 0 and never reaches power).
The road vehicle feebate of the engineer road model adds reg.rod (the road regulation shadow price) instead of the carbon price, which is in the fuel price already (prototype bug M13).
A text that is not in the table counts as explicit pricing (as the shipped ” - Carbon tax”).



3. Macros
Core buttons (green, on ScenarioCompare): Recalculate now, Recalculation on/off, Run stored scenarios, Update data tables. The others are grey, below them.

RunAllScenarios (button Run stored scenarios): stores the baseline under ID 1 if none is stored yet. Then, for every definition with Run? = Yes, it copies the definition’s inputs and name into the live scenario (skipping two formula rows), clears the ETS price override and recalculates, runs the ETS goal seek if the definition applies a new ETS without “Override ETS price” = Yes, and stores the live scenario’s outputs as values under the definition’s number and name (replacing that ID’s rows wherever they are). At the end it restores the live scenario, the override and the calculation mode it found, sorts StoredOutputs, groups the blank scenario columns and refreshes the dashboard charts.
RecalculateNow: full recalculation (timed), then the dashboard charts. The workbook ships with its values in manual calculation; ToggleRecalculation switches automatic calculation on or off (for every open workbook, as Excel does).
StoreBaseline: replaces the stored baseline with the current scenario-1 results, after a confirmation.
StoreLiveScenario: stores the live scenario as it stands, under an ID you choose (default: the next free ID from 100).
SolveETSLive: ETS goal seek for the live scenario only. It fills the override prices and switches the override on.
ClearStoredScenarios: deletes every stored scenario except the baseline.
SortStoredOutputs: sorts StoredOutputs by code stem, then ID.
GroupBlankScenarios: groups and collapses the scenario columns of ScenarioDefinition that have no name.
RefreshDashboard: rebuilds the series of the dashboard charts from the scenarios with results in the chosen source (short names in the legend, baseline dashed grey, one colour per scenario slot) and hides the table rows of the others.
CheckBatchRun: the first-run test (section 4). It reruns the batch, so the stored scenarios are recalculated by the application that runs it.

The ETS goal seek is legacy’s damped log-space iteration, as in ets_goalseek.py. It starts from the override prices, or from the fast estimate if there are none. Each step is p × (proposed price / p) ^ alpha, mixed 0.3 with the previous iterate, with 5% smoothing. Alpha halves when the error grows (minimum 0.0625) and rises ×1.2 when the error more than halves (maximum 1). It stops when the worst |covered / cap − 1| is below 0.5%, or after 20 iterations.


4. First run in Excel
The VBA project (written by vba_project.py) and the stored results were produced without Excel. They are tested in LibreOffice: the module loads, the macros reproduce the Python emulation, and CheckBatchRun passes. To confirm the same in Excel:

If the file was downloaded, unblock it first (file Properties > Unblock), or Excel opens it with macros disabled.
Open it and choose Enable Content.
Run CheckBatchRun (Alt+F8); it takes a minute or two. It checks the 12 lookups the macros rely on (sheets, rows by code, scenario columns, LiveOutputs blocks); compares Excel’s own recalculation of the baseline with the stored baseline (plain formulas only, so Excel and LibreOffice calculate it the same way); and reruns RunAllScenarios, ETS goal seek included, comparing every stored value with the value stored before.
MacroCheck shows Result PASS when no value differs by more than 1e-6 (relative). CHECK lists how many values differ; FAIL names the lookup that was not found.
If Excel cannot load the VBA project, or Alt+F8 lists no macros: remove the project if one is listed, import CPATScenarios.bas (Alt+F11 > File > Import), save as .xlsm and run CheckBatchRun again.



5. Comparing and keeping results

Source and year. On ScenarioCompare choose Results from (Stored or Live) and the year, then Recalculate now. Stored reads StoredOutputs (every stored scenario); Live reads LiveOutputs (the scenario groups of Mitigation: the baseline and the live scenario, and any group added by copy-paste). The names SCVal, SCCode and SCYear choose the range with CHOOSE; every value is INDEX(SCVal, MATCH(country.stem.ID, SCCode, 0), year column), so the order of the rows never matters.
Scenario slots. Up to 10, in ScenarioDefinition order: ID, short name (the legend), name. A scenario with no result in the chosen source shows blank (key table) or #N/A (time series, hidden by a conditional format, a gap in the charts); the charts leave it out.
Key table. Energy CO2 emissions, GHG emissions excluding LULUCF, revenue as a share of GDP, the GDP effect of the revenue use and the net welfare effect: level, difference from the baseline, and % difference for the two emission levels. The bar chart beside it shows the % difference of energy CO2 by scenario.
Time series. Four tables (default: energy CO2, GHGs, revenue, GDP effect), scenarios down and years across, each with its line chart beside it. The title of each table is a dropdown of the indicator list at the bottom of the tab: every LiveOutputs indicator except the price and Kaya indices.
StoredOutputs holds values only, so results from other files can be pasted in as values under new IDs, as long as its column layout is kept (output code in column D).
The baseline changes only when StoreBaseline is run.



6. Limits

The batch run calculates one policy scenario at a time. Further Mitigation scenario groups (copies of group 2) show on the dashboard under Live; the batch macros use the live scenario (group 2) only.
LiveOutputs (123 indicators, incl. power, fuel use and revenues with power, existing carbon pricing, GHGs, GDP effects) defines what is stored. To store more, add rows to the LiveOutputs blocks first.

B.II-B.III, C.I 528-556, I152-I237


3 Indirect prices
Category price change = Σ_f Lcat(c,f) x g_f. Lcat is the household-demand weighted Leontief coefficient (IO_GTAP table). g_f = R_f / T_f, with R_f = Σ spending x price change of the fuel group and T_f = total embedded plus own use.
C.I 496-736


4 Price factors
dp x (1 + dp)^ε (HH_Elast, decile-specific; PEDs). The exempt cooking fuel is 0 for the bottom deciles.
C.II 801-825


5 Budget shares
HHSurvey by sample, statistic (row 9) and decile.
C.III-C.IV


6 Effects
Effect = -price factor x budget share x loss scale (% of consumption, loss negative). Loss scale = behavioural factor (InferredDist: revenue / implied revenue) + DWLTri x (1 - factor) if DWLs.
C.V-C.VII, D.II


7 Rebasing
Population = survey population x population / survey population. Per-capita consumption = survey value x national consumption / (survey basket x population). National consumption = GDP x consumption share (WDI, latest year).
C.VIII


8 Recycling
PIT (personal allowance, proportional, targeted exemption). Targeted cash transfer (bottom percentile, coverage, leakage). Public investment (people without access). Current spending (ASPIRE quintiles). All per capita, then in % of each sample’s consumption.
C.X-C.XI


9 Net, compensation, Gini
Net effect = effect + recycling. Compensation share = loss x consumption / Σ. Gini = 1 - SUMPRODUCT(consumption, DGiniW) / SUM(consumption), base, after the price effects and after recycling.
C.IX, C.XII, D.V



Two identities let the sheet stay short:

Indirect prices (ScaleGTAP = Yes, legacy default).

Legacy rescales each GTAP sector’s raw price change by k(s) = Σ_f σ(f,s) R_f / Σ_f Emb(f,s) dp(f,s).
With Emb(f,s) = Y_s L(f,s) and σ(f,s) = Emb(f,s) / T_f, the sector’s adjusted change is Σ_f L(f,s) R_f / T_f. The sector-specific fuel prices cancel.
Checked on legacy’s cache: all 59 sectors to 4e-16, and the 14 categories to 3e-6 (legacy prints 6 digits).
ScaleGTAP = No uses g_f = R_f / spending_f, i.e. the economy-wide price change. Legacy instead uses the price change of each GTAP sector’s CPAT sector; that simplification is recorded.

Gini.

Legacy fits L(x) = a x² + b x to the cumulative decile shares (LINEST, no intercept) and takes Gini = (5 - area) / 5.
The fit is linear in L, so Gini = 1 - Σ_j s_j W_j with fixed weights W_j (DistMapping, name DGiniW; distribution_ref.gini_weights).
Replicated as an issue: the fitted curve, not the trapezoid rule.

title: 12  Distribution and air-pollution modules
text:
Distribution module
The mitigation prototype is the integrated model. Two further modules are standalone workbooks that take their inputs from it: the distribution module and the air-pollution module. Every module is published under <Name>_latest in excel_ai/permalink/ and excel_ai/permalink_countryeditable/, through which the modules link to each other.
The standalone distribution module (excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Distribution-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm) computes the household effects by decile of a mitigation scenario: price changes, budget shares, direct and indirect effects, revenue recycling and welfare. Its method is the Distribution tab of the mitigation prototype (Chapter 10).
One copy of the formulas. The module is cut from the built mitigation prototype: its Distribution and FromMitigation tabs, the distribution data tabs, ScenarioDefinition (distribution rows shown) and Settings. To change a formula, change the mitigation builder, rebuild the prototype, then rebuild the module.
One input tab. Its only input from Mitigation is the tab FromMitigation: the values of the prototype’s export block (section 19a, defined name ExportDistn), in the Mitigation column layout. The button Update from Mitigation on Cover copies those values from the mitigation workbook named on Cover. If that workbook is open, its current values are used; otherwise it is opened read-only, without macros or recalculation. The module runs one scenario at a time.
Build and check.
The check confirms that the Distribution tab equals the prototype’s cell for cell, that FromMitigation equals section 19a through the macro’s row mapping, that no formula reads a dropped tab or an undefined name, and, end to end, that a carbon price changed in the prototype and carried over by the update gives the same Distribution.

title: 12  Distribution and air-pollution modules
text:
Air-pollution module
The air-pollution module (excel_ai/air_pollution/) is a standalone rebuild of the Air Pollution module of legacy CPAT 1.0pre_459. It starts from the pollutant emissions produced by Mitigation and does not recalculate fuel use or emissions.
Boundary. The inputs are the baseline and policy emission series keyed by the codes aps.<pollutant>.<sector>, with year, country, unit, scenario and source traceability. In legacy 459 the handoff is country.mit.em.<pollutant>.<sector>.<scenario> in tonnes per year; the current Mitigation outputs are in kt, so units are converted explicitly at the boundary. Once the input block is filled, the workbook runs without links to another workbook.
Scope. The module reproduces the calculations and options of legacy 459: emissions to concentrations, exposure and health burden, and economic outputs, for baseline and policy scenarios and their difference. Fuel externalities are reported as outputs only and are not fed back into Mitigation prices.
Status. The current workbook holds the scaffold: Cover, Data Sources, Mitigation Inputs and the nine public reference tables extracted from legacy 459 (data/air_pollution/legacy_459/). The calculations, unit conversion, outputs and the numerical regression are open. The first regression case is Senegal, the country selected in the legacy NoPropData dashboard.
Validation. Each selected output is compared with legacy 459 by scenario and year, and every difference is classified as a confirmed bug fix, a replicated issue, or unresolved. Numerical equivalence is not claimed until the selected country has populated, reproducible inputs.

Dashboard inputs (manual inputs) can be adjusted in config.py file by modifying SCENARIOS. Each key, value pair in SCENARIOS dictionary represents name of a scenario and parameters that overwrite the default dashboard input values for this specific scenario.
Parameters that can be adjusted from the code are: selected_countries and last_simulation_year. Please do not change base_year = 2022.
Saving the results is not handled by run_model.py and can be easily implemented in a custom way by identifying the scenario via the keys in config.SCENARIOS and saving the desired variables or tables to CSV/XLSX files.

title: 16  Working in the repository
text:
Files, versions and releases
The project works under written norms (NORMS.md at the root of the repository). They bind people and AI agents alike; AGENTS.md routes any AI agent to them. This chapter summarises the norms that shape the files a reader meets; NORMS.md is the authority.
Main files carry their version. The current version of each main file sits at the top of excel_ai/ as <Name>_v<version>.<ext>, for example CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v0.9.0.xlsm:

text:

The legacy bugs, with every cell-level fix plan

The master list of bugs and issues

The code protocol, vocabularies, variables, output codes and every input

The slide deck: status, how to use it, results




Older versions move to excel_ai/releases/ when a new version is written.
excel_ai/permalink/ holds only what other files link to, under <Name>_latest: every module. excel_ai/permalink_countryeditable/ is a copy for local, country-specific runs.
Version numbers. Three parts, 0.<major>.<minor>, until the first full release 1.0.0: the last part for fixes and small features, the middle part for structural or methodological change. Each module with its own builder (distribution, air pollution) has its own version and records which mitigation version it was built from. Files released before the change to three parts were renamed; their contents keep the old two-part numbers. The register documents, the tracker and the codes map carry the version of the mitigation prototype they were made with.
One version table per workbook and generated document, in the same columns: version, date, description (with register codes), and the largest regression difference against the previous release.

text:
Checks








Check
When
What it does




Quick check (check_quick.py)
After every change; a few minutes
Structure, names, literals, formula length, a full recalculation with no error cells, the code protocol, the change of every output code against the last release


Paste test (check_paste.py)
Every release
Pastes the live scenario’s column group into further groups, as a user would, and checks that the pasted groups number themselves, show no errors and reproduce the stored results


Full check (check_full.py)
At a milestone; several hours
Everything, including the macro tests


Independent recomputation
Within the checks
Python reference models of the power, transport and distribution blocks reproduce the workbook’s numbers



Every increment is a regression test: the new version’s values are compared with the previous release, and every difference is zero or explained in the version table.

title: 16  Working in the repository
text:
Excel written by code
The Excel prototypes are written with openpyxl and recalculated in LibreOffice, so they build and check on Linux and in cloud sessions. Excel 365 is used for review only. The norms set the column layout of every sheet type, a visual style guide (colours, fonts, borders, sections), formula rules (at most 100 characters; one formula serves a whole block), copy-paste ability of scenario columns, and lint rules that every file passes before it ships so Excel never shows a repair prompt.

title: 16  Working in the repository
text:
Task completion
Every finished task ends with an entry at the bottom of CAVEATS.md, the single record of completed work: the task, its inputs, its outputs and its caveats. Earlier entries may be corrected but not deleted. Open work is listed in excel_ai/plans/TODO.md and coded/TODO.md.
Norms follow the lessons. A mistake whose cause could recur ends with a norm and a check that would have caught it, added in the same task.
